---
title: "Longitudinal Trajectories of Physical Activity"
subtitle: "A 4-Year Longitudinal Analysis of Accelerometry Outcomes"
author:
  - name: "Jesús del Pozo Cruz"
    affiliation: "University of Seville"
    email: "jpozo2@us.es"
  - name: "Daniel Gallardo Gómez"
    affiliation: "ICON Clinical Research"
    email: "daniel.gallardo@iconplc.com"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%B %d, %Y')`"
output:
  html_document:
    theme: flatly
    highlight: tango
    toc: true
    toc_float:
      collapsed: true
      smooth_scroll: true
    toc_depth: 3
    number_sections: true
    code_folding: hide
    df_print: paged
    self_contained: true
  word_document:
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 3
  pdf_document:
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 3
    number_sections: true
    latex_engine: xelatex
abstract: |
  Background:
  Accelerometry enables objective assessment of multiple complementary dimensions of physical activity, including overall volume, accumulated duration, and intensity-related performance. Understanding how these dimensions change longitudinally is essential for informing ageing-related physical activity research and intervention strategies.

  Methods:
  We analysed four repeated accelerometry measurement waves over approximately four years using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes. Time (years), centred baseline age, and sex were included as fixed effects, while participant-level random effects accounted for within-person correlation. Three accelerometry-derived outcomes were examined: daily steps, daily walking time (minutes/day), and peak 30-minute cadence (steps/min). Sensitivity analyses included fixed-effects (within-person) models and Bayesian hierarchical models, with model comparison based on leave-one-out cross-validation.

  Results:
  Across all three outcomes, time was consistently associated with within-person declines in physical activity. Daily steps decreased by approximately 251 steps per year, daily walking time declined by 3.0 minutes per year, and peak 30-minute cadence decreased by 1.43 steps/min per year. Baseline age was negatively associated with all outcomes, while sex differences were modest in magnitude and outcome-specific. Substantial between-person heterogeneity was observed in both baseline levels and longitudinal trajectories. Fixed-effects and Bayesian sensitivity analyses yielded concordant results, supporting the robustness of the primary mixed-effects findings.

  Conclusions:
  Complementary frequentist and Bayesian longitudinal modelling approaches provide robust evidence of within-person declines across volume-, time-, and intensity-related accelerometry-derived activity metrics. Joint consideration of these dimensions offers a more comprehensive understanding of longitudinal physical activity patterns with ageing.
keywords: "accelerometry; steps; walking time; cadence; mixed-effects models; fixed-effects; Bayesian analysis; longitudinal"
---
# Data and global setup
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Global chunk options
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  eval = FALSE,
  echo = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 6,
  dpi = 300,
  fig.align = "center",
  cache = FALSE,
  comment = "##"
)

# Create output directory for figures and tables
out_dir <- "outputs"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) {
  dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PORTABILITY SHIM (repo) -- makes all paths repo-relative & machine-independent
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Output subdirectories
fig_dir <- file.path(out_dir, "figures")
tab_dir <- file.path(out_dir, "tables")
for (d in c(fig_dir, tab_dir)) if (!dir.exists(d)) dir.create(d, recursive = TRUE)

# Route EVERY ggsave() to outputs/figures by basename, regardless of the path
# written in the original call (absolute paths, "walk/..", bare names all work).
if (!isTRUE(getOption("repo_ggsave_wrapped"))) {
  .orig_ggsave <- ggplot2::ggsave
  ggsave <- function(filename, ...) .orig_ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, basename(filename)), ...)
  options(repo_ggsave_wrapped = TRUE)
}

# Portable data path: env DATA_PATH > data/raw/df.csv > data/synthetic/df_synthetic.csv
resolve_data_path <- function() {
  cand <- c(Sys.getenv("DATA_PATH", unset = NA),
            "../data/raw/df.csv", "data/raw/df.csv", "df.csv",
            "../data/synthetic/df_synthetic.csv", "data/synthetic/df_synthetic.csv")
  cand <- cand[!is.na(cand)]
  hit <- cand[file.exists(cand)]
  if (length(hit) == 0)
    stop("No data file found. Place the NHATS-derived df.csv in data/raw/ (see data/raw/README.md) or generate the synthetic sample.")
  if (grepl("synthetic", hit[1]))
    message("NOTE: using SYNTHETIC sample data (", hit[1], "). Results are illustrative only, not the published estimates.")
  hit[1]
}

# Custom ggplot2 theme
theme_publication <- function(base_size = 13, base_family = "") {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.2), face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = rel(1), hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = rel(0.8), hjust = 1, face = "italic"),
      axis.title = element_text(size = rel(1.1), face = "bold"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.9)),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, color = "grey70"),
      strip.text = element_text(size = rel(1), face = "bold"),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90", color = "grey70")
    )
}

# Set default theme
theme_set(theme_publication())

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# TableOne by WAVE with SMD (no p-values) + Word export (JAMA style)
# MODIFICATION INCLUDED:
#   - addOverall = TRUE (adds Overall column)
#   - caption includes N
#   - wave included as factor variable (and also appears in the table)
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(dplyr)
library(tableone)
library(officer)
library(flextable)
library(tibble)

# -----------------------------
# Helpers (JAMA-ish / booktabs)
# -----------------------------

is_level_row <- function(x) grepl("^\\s{2,}", x)

indent_levels <- function(ft, df, col = "Characteristic") {
  lvl <- is_level_row(df[[col]])
  if (any(lvl)) {
    ft <- padding(ft, i = which(lvl), j = 1, padding.left = 20, part = "body")
  }
  ft
}

jamatabs_style <- function(ft) {
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline_top(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- hline(ft, border = fp_border(width = 0.8), part = "header")
  ft <- hline_bottom(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")

  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 10, part = "all")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- valign(ft, valign = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding = 2, part = "all")
  ft
}

tableone_to_df <- function(tab_print) {
  df <- as.data.frame(tab_print, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
    rownames_to_column("Characteristic")
  rownames(df) <- NULL
  df
}

make_jama_ft_tableone <- function(df, caption) {
  ft <- flextable(df)

  # Left align first col, right align rest
  ft <- align(ft, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
  if (ncol(df) >= 2) {
    ft <- align(ft, j = 2:ncol(df), align = "right", part = "all")
  }

  ft <- jamatabs_style(ft)
  ft <- autofit(ft)
  ft <- indent_levels(ft, df, col = "Characteristic")
  ft <- set_caption(ft, caption = caption)

  ft
}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Retain only valid accelerometry measurements
# ------------------------------------------------------------
df_acc <- df %>%
  filter(
    accelerometer == 1,
    !is.na(Steps_ponderada)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Make wave a labeled factor
    wave = factor(
      wave,
      levels = c(11, 12, 13, 14),
      labels = c("Wave 11", "Wave 12", "Wave 13", "Wave 14")
    )
  )

N_total <- nrow(df_acc)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Build labeled TableOne dataset (include wave!)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
table1data <- df_acc %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Steps_ponderada,
    Walk_mins_ponderada,
    CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada,
    sisindex,
    res,
    income,
    frailty_category,
    age,
    sex,
    bmi,
    wave
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex,
                 levels = c(1, 2),
                 labels = c("Male", "Female")),

    income = factor(income,
                    levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                    labels = c("<$14k",
                               "$14k–$22k",
                               "$22k–$36k",
                               "$36k–$49k",
                               ">$49k")),

    res = factor(res,
                 levels = c(1, 2),
                 labels = c("Community", "Other")),

    frailty_category = factor(frailty_category,
                              levels = c(0, 1, 2),
                              labels = c("No frailty",
                                         "Mild frailty",
                                         "Moderate–severe frailty"))
  )

# Optional: collapse social isolation to categories (recommended)
table1data <- table1data %>%
  mutate(
    sociso_cat = case_when(
      sisindex %in% c(0, 1) ~ "Well connected (0–1)",
      sisindex %in% c(2, 3, 4) ~ "Partially isolated (2–4)",
      sisindex %in% c(5, 6) ~ "Severely isolated (5–6)",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    sociso_cat = factor(
      sociso_cat,
      levels = c("Well connected (0–1)",
                 "Partially isolated (2–4)",
                 "Severely isolated (5–6)")
    )
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Create TableOne stratified by wave WITH Overall + SMD (no p-values)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
vars <- c(
  "wave",  # include wave itself as a row
  "Steps_ponderada",
  "Walk_mins_ponderada",
  "CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada",
  "sociso_cat",
  "res",
  "income",
  "frailty_category",
  "age",
  "sex",
  "bmi"
)

factorVars <- c("wave", "sociso_cat", "res", "income", "frailty_category", "sex")

nonnormalVars <- c("Steps_ponderada",
                   "Walk_mins_ponderada",
                   "CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada",
                   "bmi")

tab_wave <- CreateTableOne(
  vars = vars,
  strata = "wave",
  data = table1data,
  factorVars = factorVars,
  addOverall = TRUE
)

tab_wave_print <- print(
  tab_wave,
  nonnormal = nonnormalVars,
  smd = TRUE,     # adds SMD
  test = FALSE,   # removes p-values/tests
  quote = FALSE,
  noSpaces = TRUE
)

df_wave <- tableone_to_df(tab_wave_print)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4) Word export
# ------------------------------------------------------------
ft_wave <- make_jama_ft_tableone(
  df_wave,
  caption = paste0(
    "Table 1. Participant characteristics by measurement wave (Overall and SMD; N = ",
    format(N_total, big.mark = ","),
    ")"
  )
)

# Optional footnote lines
ft_wave <- add_footer_lines(
  ft_wave,
  values = c(
    "Values are n (%) unless otherwise indicated.",
    "Continuous variables are mean (SD) or median [IQR] as specified.",
    "SMD = standardized mean difference."
  )
) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_docx <- file.path(tab_dir, "Table1.docx")

# safer (no pipe) to avoid quote/encoding issues
doc <- read_docx()
doc <- body_add_par(doc, "Tables", style = "heading 1")
doc <- body_add_par(doc, "", style = "Normal")
doc <- body_add_flextable(doc, ft_wave)

print(doc, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_docx)))

out_docx

```{r create-variables, eval=TRUE}
df_mod <- df_acc %>%
  mutate(
    # Factor encoding
    id = factor(id),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("1", "2"), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    
    # Temporal variable
    wave_num = as.integer(wave),
    time = wave_num - min(wave_num, na.rm = TRUE)  # Time in years from baseline
  ) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    # Baseline characteristics (time-invariant)
    age_baseline = first(age, order_by = wave_num)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    # Centered age (improves interpretability and reduces collinearity)
    age_c = as.numeric(scale(age_baseline, scale = FALSE))
  )

# Display variable summary
summary_vars <- df_mod %>%
  select(Steps_ponderada,Walk_mins_ponderada, CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada, time, age_baseline, age_c, sex) %>%
  summary()

print(summary_vars)
```

# Outcome 1: Daily steps


# Introduction

Physical activity is a critical determinant of health across the lifespan. Accelerometry provides objective, continuous measures of movement, enabling precise characterization of daily activity patterns. Understanding how physical activity evolves over time—and how these trajectories differ across demographic groups—is essential for developing evidence-based interventions.

## Study Objectives

This analysis examines:

1. **Temporal trends**: Changes in daily steps over a 4-year observation period
2. **Demographic differences**: Sex-specific trajectories adjusted for baseline age
3. **Within-person dynamics**: Individual-level variation using mixed-effects modeling
4. **Model validation**: Sensitivity analyses using frequentist models (i.e., linear-mixed, and OLS models) to test the robustness of our base-case (Bayesian model)

<div class="technical-note">
**Technical Approach:** We employ a hierarchical modeling framework that accounts for the nested structure of repeated measurements within individuals. This approach provides efficient estimation of population-level trends while appropriately quantifying uncertainty propagation to predictions at both the individual and population levels.
</div>

---

# Methods

## Data Structure and Preparation


<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Data Structure:** The dataset contains `r nrow(df)` observations from `r n_distinct(df$id)` unique participants measured across `r n_distinct(df$wave)` waves. Each row represents a single measurement occasion (person-wave combination), forming a **long-format** longitudinal dataset suitable for mixed-effects modeling.
</div>

## Sample Selection


<div class="interpretation">
**Sample Retention:** The analysis includes `r nrow(df_acc)` valid accelerometry observations. Attrition patterns will be assessed in sensitivity analyses to evaluate potential selection bias.
</div>

## Variable Construction


<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Centering Rationale:** Age was mean-centered (M = `r round(mean(df_mod$age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` years) to facilitate interpretation of the intercept as the expected outcome at mean age and baseline time. This transformation does not affect slope estimates but improves numerical stability and reduces multicollinearity between main effects and potential interactions.
</div>

---

# Descriptive Statistics

## Sample Characteristics

```{r steps_descriptive-table, eval=TRUE}
# Compute comprehensive descriptive statistics
desc_overall <- df_mod %>%
  summarise(
    N_observations = n(),
    N_participants = n_distinct(id),
    Mean_age = mean(age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_age = sd(age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min_age = min(age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max_age = max(age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

desc_by_sex <- df_mod %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(
    N_participants = n_distinct(id),
    Mean_age = mean(age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_age = sd(age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(
  desc_overall,
  caption = "**Table 2.** Overall sample characteristics",
  digits = 1,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
) %>%

kable(

```{r steps_descriptive-steps}
## Physical Activity by Wave

# Compute mean and SD by wave
tab_desc <- df_mod %>%
  group_by(wave_num) %>%
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean_steps = mean(Steps_ponderada, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_steps = sd(Steps_ponderada, na.rm = TRUE),
    SE_steps = SD_steps / sqrt(N),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(
  tab_desc,
  caption = "**Table 4.** Daily steps by measurement wave",
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Wave", "N", "Mean", "SD", "SE"),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )

```{r steps_plot-observed-steps, fig.cap="**Figure 1.** Observed mean daily steps across measurement waves. Error bars represent ±1 SE.", eval=TRUE}
p_obs <- ggplot(df_mod, aes(x = wave_num, y = Steps_ponderada)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.2,
    linewidth = 0.8,
    color = "grey40"
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "line",
    linewidth = 1.2,
    color = "#3498db"
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    size = 3,
    color = "#3498db",
    fill = "white",
    shape = 21,
    stroke = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma_format(),
    breaks = seq(0, 10000, 100)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(df_mod$wave_num)) +
  labs(
    x = "Measurement Wave",

    subtitle = "Unadjusted observed means across four measurement waves"
  )

print(p_obs)

# Export figure
ggsave(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, "Figure_1_observed_steps.png"),
  plot = p_obs,
  width = 9,

# Sensitivity Analysis: Linear Mixed-Effects Model

## Model Specification

The primary analytical model is a **linear mixed-effects model** with random intercepts and slopes:

$$
\text{Steps}_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Time}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Age}_i + \beta_3 \text{Sex}_i + b_{0i} + b_{1i} \text{Time}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$

Where:

- $\text{Steps}_{ij}$ is the daily step count for individual $i$ at time $j$
- $\beta_0$ is the population-level intercept
- $\beta_1$ is the population-level slope for time (years)
- $\beta_2$ is the effect of baseline age (centered)
- $\beta_3$ is the sex difference (reference: Male)
- $b_{0i} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{b_0})$ is the random intercept for individual $i$
- $b_{1i} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{b_1})$ is the random slope for individual $i$
- $\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ is the residual error

<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Model Justification:**

1. **Random Intercepts:** Allow each individual to have their own baseline step count, accounting for time-invariant individual differences
2. **Random Slopes:** Allow the rate of change over time to vary across individuals, capturing heterogeneity in trajectories
3. **REML Estimation:** Restricted Maximum Likelihood provides unbiased estimates of variance components and is preferred for unbalanced designs
4. **Covariance Structure:** We allow correlation between random intercepts and slopes, acknowledging that baseline levels may predict rates of change
</div>

## Model Estimation

```{r steps_main-model, eval=TRUE}
# Fit linear mixed-effects model
m_main_steps <- lme(
  fixed = Steps_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex,
  random = ~ time | id,
  data = df_mod,
  method = "REML",
  control = lmeControl(
    opt = "optim",
    maxIter = 100,
    msMaxIter = 100
  ),
  na.action = na.omit
)

# Model summary
summary(m_main_steps)

# Extract fixed effects
fixed_effects <- summary(m_main_steps)$tTable
fixed_effects_df <- as.data.frame(fixed_effects) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Parameter") %>%
  mutate(
    `95% CI Lower` = Value - 1.96 * Std.Error,
    `95% CI Upper` = Value + 1.96 * Std.Error,
    `p-value` = `p-value`
  )

kable(
  fixed_effects_df,
  caption = "**Table 5.** Fixed effects estimates from linear mixed-effects model (Daily Steps)",
  digits = c(0, 2, 2, 0, 3, 2, 2),
  col.names = c("Parameter", "Estimate", "SE", "DF", "t-value", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper", "p-value"),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )

# Extract random effects variance components
random_effects <- VarCorr(m_main_steps)
random_effects_df <- data.frame(
  Component = c("Intercept SD", "Slope SD", "Correlation", "Residual SD"),
  Estimate = c(
    as.numeric(random_effects["(Intercept)", "StdDev"]),
    as.numeric(random_effects["time", "StdDev"]),
    as.numeric(random_effects["time", "Corr"]),
    as.numeric(random_effects["Residual", "StdDev"])
  )
)

kable(
  random_effects_df,
  caption = "**Table 6.** Random effects variance components",
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Variance Component", "Estimate")
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )
##tables to word
library(officer)
library(flextable)
library(dplyr)

# -----------------------------
# JAMA-style formatting helper
# -----------------------------
jamatabs_style <- function(ft) {
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline_top(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- hline(ft, border = fp_border(width = 0.8), part = "header")
  ft <- hline_bottom(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 10, part = "all")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- valign(ft, valign = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding = 2, part = "all")
  ft <- autofit(ft)
  ft
}

# Safe numeric formatter (avoids ultra-long zeros)
fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    NA_character_,
    formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = digits)
  )
}

# p-value formatter (keeps small p as "<0.001")
fmt_p <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  out <- ifelse(is.na(x), NA_character_, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits))
  out[!is.na(x) & x < 0.001] <- "<0.001"
  out
}

make_jama_ft <- function(df, caption) {
  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- align(ft, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
  if (ncol(df) >= 2) ft <- align(ft, j = 2:ncol(df), align = "right", part = "all")
  ft <- jamatabs_style(ft)
  ft <- set_caption(ft, caption = caption)
  ft
}

    # common column names from your object:

  )

# If your columns are exactly these names (as in your chunk), format them:

<div class="interpretation">
**Model Results Interpretation:**

- **Time Effect:** $\beta_{\text{time}}$ = `r round(fixef(m_main_steps)["time"], 1)` steps/year (95% CI: [`r paste(round(fixed_effects_df$"95% CI Lower"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"], 1), round(fixed_effects_df$"95% CI Upper"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"], 1), sep = ", ")`], *p* `r { { if(fixed_effects_df$"p-value"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"] < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste0("= ", round(fixed_effects_df$"p-value"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"], 3)) } }`)
  - This represents the average annual change in daily steps, holding age and sex constant
  
- **Age Effect:** $\beta_{\text{age}}$ = `r round(fixef(m_main_steps)["age_c"], 1)` steps per year of age
  - Each additional year of baseline age is associated with `r abs(round(fixef(m_main_steps)["age_c"], 1))` `r { { if(fixef(m_main_steps)["age_c"] > 0) "more" else "fewer" } }` daily steps
  
- **Sex Difference:** $\beta_{\text{sex}}$ = `r round(fixef(m_main_steps)["sexFemale"], 1)` steps
  - Females average `r abs(round(fixef(m_main_steps)["sexFemale"], 1))` `r { { if(fixef(m_main_steps)["sexFemale"] > 0) "more" else "fewer" } }` daily steps than males, adjusted for age and time

- **Between-Person Variability:** SD(Intercept) = `r round(as.numeric(random_effects["(Intercept)", "StdDev"]), 1)` steps
  - Substantial individual differences in baseline activity levels
  
- **Within-Person Variability:** SD(Slope) = `r round(as.numeric(random_effects["time", "StdDev"]), 1)` steps/year
  - Individuals vary considerably in their rates of change over time
  
- **Intercept-Slope Correlation:** $r$ = `r round(as.numeric(random_effects["time", "Corr"]), 2)`
  - `r { { if(as.numeric(random_effects["time", "Corr"]) > 0) "Positive correlation suggests that individuals with higher baseline steps tend to show faster increases over time" else "Negative correlation suggests that individuals with higher baseline steps tend to show slower increases (or greater decreases) over time" } }`
</div>


# Sensitivity Analysis: Fixed-Effects Models

Fixed-effects (FE) models provide a complementary within-person perspective by controlling for all time-invariant individual characteristics—both measured and unmeasured. These models estimate effects using **only within-person variation**, eliminating confounding from stable individual differences.

<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Fixed-Effects Advantages:**

1. **Unmeasured confounding control:** Automatically adjusts for all time-invariant individual characteristics
2. **Causal inference:** Under weaker assumptions, FE estimates have a stronger causal interpretation
3. **Robustness:** Less sensitive to between-person confounding and selection bias

**Trade-offs:**

1. **Cannot estimate time-invariant effects:** Sex, baseline age effects are absorbed into individual fixed effects
2. **Less efficient:** Uses only within-person variation, discarding between-person information
3. **Sensitive to measurement error:** Differencing amplifies noise in predictors
</div>

## Data Preparation for FE Models

```{r steps_fe-data-prep, eval=TRUE}
# Create within-person deviations
df_fe <- df_mod %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    # Within-person age deviation (time-varying component)
    age_w = age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Summary of within-person age variation
summary(df_fe$age_w)
```

## Spline FE Model with Bootstrap CIs

```{r Figure_S1_FE_spline_bootstrap, fig.cap="Figure S1. Within-person trajectory using a fixed-effects model with natural splines (df = 3). Shaded area represents cluster bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## Spline FE Model with Bootstrap CIs
library(fixest)
library(splines)
library(ggplot2)

# Ensure output directory exists
if (!dir.exists("outputs")) dir.create("outputs")

# Fit FE spline model
fe_spline <- feols(
  Steps_ponderada ~ ns(time, df = 3) | id,
  data = df_fe,
  cluster = "id"
)

# --- Helper: manual Xβ prediction (no fixed effects needed) ---
predict_xb_ns3 <- function(model, newdata){
  X <- model.matrix(~ ns(time, df = 3), data = newdata)
  # Drop intercept to match fixest coef (usually no intercept with FE)
  if ("(Intercept)" %in% colnames(X)) X <- X[, colnames(X) != "(Intercept)", drop = FALSE]

  b <- coef(model)
  # Align columns just in case
  X <- X[, names(b), drop = FALSE]
  as.numeric(X %*% b)
}

# Prediction grid
time_min <- min(df_fe$time, na.rm = TRUE)
time_max <- max(df_fe$time, na.rm = TRUE)
grid_time <- data.frame(time = seq(time_min, time_max, length.out = 100))

# Point estimate (Xβ)
fit_hat <- predict_xb_ns3(fe_spline, grid_time)

# Cluster bootstrap (resample individuals)
set.seed(123)
B <- 500
ids <- unique(df_fe$id)

pred_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = nrow(grid_time), ncol = B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  samp_ids <- sample(ids, length(ids), replace = TRUE)
  boot_df <- df_fe[df_fe$id %in% samp_ids, , drop = FALSE]

  # Re-label duplicated IDs so FE works under resampling-with-replacement
  boot_df$id_boot <- paste0(boot_df$id, "_", ave(boot_df$id, boot_df$id, FUN = seq_along))

  m_b <- feols(
    Steps_ponderada ~ ns(time, df = 3) | id_boot,
    data = boot_df,
    cluster = "id_boot"
  )

  pred_mat[, b] <- predict_xb_ns3(m_b, grid_time)
}

# Bootstrap CIs
lo <- apply(pred_mat, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
hi <- apply(pred_mat, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)

grid_s <- data.frame(time = grid_time$time, fit = fit_hat, lo = lo, hi = hi)

# Plot
p_fes <- ggplot(grid_s, aes(x = time, y = fit)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.20) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Daily Steps (within-person estimate)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_fes

# Export PNG
ggsave(
  filename = file.path("outputs", "Figure_S1_FE_spline_bootstrap_daily_steps.png"),
  plot = p_fes,
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

# Bayesian Hierarchical Models

Bayesian hierarchical models provide several advantages for longitudinal analysis:

1. **Full uncertainty quantification:** Posterior distributions capture all sources of uncertainty
2. **Flexible prior specification:** Can incorporate external information or enforce regularization
3. **Complex model structures:** Natural framework for hierarchical data
4. **Interpretable predictions:** Posterior predictive distributions for future observations

## Model Specifications

We fit three competing Bayesian models to evaluate potential interactions:

### Model 1: Additive Effects (Baseline)

$$
\text{Steps}_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma)
$$
$$
\mu_{ij} = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{Time}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Age}_i + \beta_3 \text{Sex}_i + b_{0i} + b_{1i} \text{Time}_{ij}
$$

### Model 2: Time × Sex Interaction

$$
\mu_{ij} = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{Time}_{ij} \times \text{Sex}_i + \beta_2 \text{Age}_i + b_{0i} + b_{1i} \text{Time}_{ij}
$$

### Model 3: Time × Age Interaction

$$
\mu_{ij} = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{Time}_{ij} \times \text{Age}_i + \beta_2 \text{Sex}_i + b_{0i} + b_{1i} \text{Time}_{ij}
$$


```{r steps_bayesian-models, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}

library(dplyr)
library(brms)

# Ensure output directory exists
if (!exists("out_dir")) out_dir <- "outputs"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir)

## Model Fitting

# setting more informative priors
priors <- c(
  prior(normal(6000, 2000), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 500), class = "b"),
  prior(exponential(0.01), class = "sd"),
  prior(exponential(0.001), class = "sigma"),
  prior(lkj(2), class = "cor")
)

# variables selection (make sure id and sex are factors)
df_mod_bay <- df_mod %>%
  select(id, Steps_ponderada, age_c, time, sex) %>%
  mutate(
    id = as.factor(id),
    sex = as.factor(sex)
  )

# Model 1: Additive effects
bayes_model_add_steps <- brm(
  formula = bf(Steps_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time + sex + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod_bay,
  family = gaussian(),
  # prior = priors,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = min(4, parallel::detectCores()),
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_add_steps")
)

# Model 2: Time × Sex interaction
bayes_model_time_sex_steps <- brm(
  formula = bf(Steps_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time:sex + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod_bay,
  family = gaussian(),
  # prior = priors,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = min(4, parallel::detectCores()),
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_time_sex_steps")
)

# Model 3: Time × Age interaction
bayes_model_time_age_steps <- brm(
  formula = bf(Steps_ponderada ~ 1 + time:age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod_bay,
  family = gaussian(),
  # prior = priors,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = min(4, parallel::detectCores()),
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_time_age_steps")
)

# Model 4: skew normal distribution
bayes_model_beta_steps <- brm(
  formula = bf(Steps_ponderada ~ 1 + time:sex + age_c + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod_bay,
  family = skew_normal(),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = min(4, parallel::detectCores()),
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_beta_steps")
)

# Outcome 2: Daily walking time

# Introduction

Walking time is a key component of daily physical activity and a strong predictor of health outcomes across the lifespan. Accelerometry allows objective and continuous quantification of walking behavior, providing detailed information on the duration of ambulatory activity in free-living conditions. Understanding how daily walking time changes over time—and whether these trajectories differ across demographic groups—is essential for informing targeted and evidence-based interventions.

## Study Objectives

This analysis examines:

1. **Temporal trends**: Changes in daily walking time over a 4-year observation period  
2. **Demographic differences**: Sex-specific walking trajectories adjusted for baseline age  
3. **Within-person dynamics**: Individual-level variation in walking time using mixed-effects modeling  
4. **Model validation**: Sensitivity analyses using fixed-effects and Bayesian approaches  

<div class="technical-note">
<strong>Technical Approach:</strong>  
We employ a hierarchical modeling framework that accounts for the nested structure of repeated walking time measurements within individuals. This approach enables efficient estimation of population-level trends while appropriately quantifying uncertainty at both the individual and population levels.
</div>

---

# Methods

## Data Structure and Preparation


<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Data Structure:** The dataset contains `r nrow(df)` observations from `r n_distinct(df$id)` unique participants measured across `r n_distinct(df$wave)` waves. Each row represents a single measurement occasion (person-wave combination), forming a **long-format** longitudinal dataset suitable for mixed-effects modeling.
</div>

## Sample Selection


<div class="interpretation">
**Sample Retention:** The analysis includes `r nrow(df_acc)` valid accelerometry observations. Attrition patterns will be assessed in sensitivity analyses to evaluate potential selection bias.
</div>

## Variable Construction


<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Centering Rationale:** Age was mean-centered (M = `r round(mean(df_mod$age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` years) to facilitate interpretation of the intercept as the expected outcome at mean age and baseline time. This transformation does not affect slope estimates but improves numerical stability and reduces multicollinearity between main effects and potential interactions.
</div>

---

# Sensitivity Analysis: Mixed-Effects Model

## Model Specification

The primary analytical model is a **linear mixed-effects model** with random intercepts and slopes:

$$
\text{WalkingMinutes
}_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Time}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Age}_i + \beta_3 \text{Sex}_i + b_{0i} + b_{1i} \text{Time}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$

Where:

- $\text{WalkingMinutes}_{ij}$ is the **daily walking time (minutes, weighted)** for individual $i$ at measurement occasion $j$
- $\beta_0$ is the **population-level intercept**, representing expected daily walking minutes at baseline time for a male participant at mean-centered age
- $\beta_1$ is the **population-level annual rate of change** in walking minutes
- $\beta_2$ is the effect of **baseline age (mean-centered)**
- $\beta_3$ represents the **sex difference** in walking minutes (reference category: Male)
- $b_{0i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{b_0})$ is the **random intercept**, allowing individuals to differ in baseline walking time
- $b_{1i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{b_1})$ is the **random slope for time**, allowing individual-specific rates of change
- $\varepsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ is the residual error term

<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Model Justification:**

1. **Random Intercepts:** Allow each individual to have their own baseline step count, accounting for time-invariant individual differences
2. **Random Slopes:** Allow the rate of change over time to vary across individuals, capturing heterogeneity in trajectories
3. **REML Estimation:** Restricted Maximum Likelihood provides unbiased estimates of variance components and is preferred for unbalanced designs
4. **Covariance Structure:** We allow correlation between random intercepts and slopes, acknowledging that baseline levels may predict rates of change
</div>



```{r walk_main-model, eval=TRUE}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# MODEL + TABLE W3 (Fixed) + TABLE W4 (Random) — DAILY WALKING TIME
# Outcome: Walk_mins_ponderada
# Exports:
#  - outputs/Table_W3_fixed_effects_walking.docx
#  - outputs/Table_W4_random_effects_walking.docx
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(nlme)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# -----------------------------
# JAMA-style formatting helper
# -----------------------------
jamatabs_style <- function(ft) {
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline_top(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- hline(ft, border = fp_border(width = 0.8), part = "header")
  ft <- hline_bottom(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 10, part = "all")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- valign(ft, valign = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding = 2, part = "all")
  ft <- autofit(ft)
  ft
}

# Safe numeric formatter
fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  ifelse(is.na(x), NA_character_, formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = digits))
}

# p-value formatter
fmt_p <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  out <- ifelse(is.na(x), NA_character_, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits))
  out[!is.na(x) & x < 0.001] <- "<0.001"
  out
}

make_jama_ft <- function(df, caption) {
  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- align(ft, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
  if (ncol(df) >= 2) ft <- align(ft, j = 2:ncol(df), align = "right", part = "all")
  ft <- jamatabs_style(ft)
  ft <- set_caption(ft, caption = caption)
  ft
}

# -----------------------------
# Fit linear mixed-effects model
# -----------------------------
m_main_walk <- lme(
  fixed = Walk_mins_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex,
  random = ~ time | id,
  data = df_mod,
  method = "REML",
  control = lmeControl(
    opt = "optim",
    maxIter = 100,
    msMaxIter = 100
  ),
  na.action = na.omit
)

summary(m_main_walk)

# -----------------------------
# Table W3 — Fixed effects
# -----------------------------
fixed_effects <- summary(m_main_walk)$tTable

fixed_effects_df <- as.data.frame(fixed_effects) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Parameter") %>%
  mutate(
    `95% CI Lower` = Value - 1.96 * Std.Error,
    `95% CI Upper` = Value + 1.96 * Std.Error
  ) %>%
  rename(
    Estimate = Value,
    SE = Std.Error
  )

fixed_W3 <- fixed_effects_df %>%
  mutate(
    DF = as.integer(round(as.numeric(DF))),
    Estimate = fmt_num(Estimate, 2),
    SE = fmt_num(SE, 2),
    `t-value` = fmt_num(`t-value`, 2),
    `95% CI Lower` = fmt_num(`95% CI Lower`, 2),
    `95% CI Upper` = fmt_num(`95% CI Upper`, 2),
    `p-value` = fmt_p(`p-value`, 3)
  )

ft_W3 <- make_jama_ft(
  fixed_W3,
  caption = "Table W3. Fixed effects estimates from linear mixed-effects model (Daily Walking Time)"
)

ft_W3 <- add_footer_lines(
  ft_W3,
  values = c(
    "Values are estimates from a linear mixed-effects model with random intercept and random time slope by participant (id).",
    "Fixed effects: time (years), centered age (age_c), and sex.",
    "95% CIs computed as Estimate ± 1.96 × SE.",
    "REML estimation used."
  )
) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_W3 <- file.path(tab_dir, "Table_W3_fixed_effects_walking.docx")

doc_W3 <- read_docx()
doc_W3 <- body_add_par(doc_W3, "Table W3", style = "heading 1")
doc_W3 <- body_add_par(doc_W3, "", style = "Normal")
doc_W3 <- body_add_flextable(doc_W3, ft_W3)
print(doc_W3, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_W3)))

out_W3

# -----------------------------
# Table W4 — Random effects
# -----------------------------
random_effects <- VarCorr(m_main_walk)

random_effects_df <- data.frame(
  Component = c("Intercept SD", "Slope SD (time)", "Correlation (Intercept–Slope)", "Residual SD"),
  Estimate = c(
    as.numeric(random_effects["(Intercept)", "StdDev"]),
    as.numeric(random_effects["time", "StdDev"]),
    as.numeric(random_effects["time", "Corr"]),
    as.numeric(random_effects["Residual", "StdDev"])
  )
)

random_W4 <- random_effects_df %>%
  mutate(Estimate = fmt_num(Estimate, 3))

ft_W4 <- make_jama_ft(
  random_W4,
  caption = "Table W4. Random effects variance components (Daily Walking Time)"
)

ft_W4 <- add_footer_lines(
  ft_W4,
  values = c(
    "Variance components from the same linear mixed-effects model.",
    "Random effects structure: random intercept and random time slope by participant (id).",
    "SD indicates standard deviation."
  )
) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_W4 <- file.path(tab_dir, "Table_W4_random_effects_walking.docx")

doc_W4 <- read_docx()
doc_W4 <- body_add_par(doc_W4, "Table W4", style = "heading 1")
doc_W4 <- body_add_par(doc_W4, "", style = "Normal")
doc_W4 <- body_add_flextable(doc_W4, ft_W4)
print(doc_W4, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_W4)))

out_W4
```

<div class="interpretation">
**Model Results Interpretation:**

- **Time Effect:** $\beta_{\text{time}}$ = `r round(fixef(m_main_walk)["time"], 1)` minutes/year 
  (95% CI: [`r paste( round(fixed_effects_df$"95% CI Lower"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"], 1), round(fixed_effects_df$"95% CI Upper"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"], 1), sep = ", " )`], *p* `r { { if(fixed_effects_df$"p-value"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"] < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste0("= ", round(fixed_effects_df$"p-value"[fixed_effects_df$Parameter == "time"], 3)) } }`)
  - This represents the average **annual change in daily walking time**, holding age and sex constant
  
- **Age Effect:** $\beta_{\text{age}}$ = `r round(fixef(m_main_walk)["age_c"], 1)` minutes per year of age
  - Each additional year of baseline age is associated with `r abs(round(fixef(m_main_walk)["age_c"], 1))` 
    `r { { if(fixef(m_main_walk)["age_c"] > 0) "more" else "fewer" } }` daily walking minutes
  
- **Sex Difference:** $\beta_{\text{sex}}$ = `r round(fixef(m_main_walk)["sexFemale"], 1)` minutes
  - Females average `r abs(round(fixef(m_main_walk)["sexFemale"], 1))` 
    `r { { if(fixef(m_main_walk)["sexFemale"] > 0) "more" else "fewer" } }` daily walking minutes than males, adjusted for age and time

- **Between-Person Variability:** SD(Intercept) = `r round(as.numeric(random_effects["(Intercept)", "StdDev"]), 1)` minutes
  - Substantial individual differences in baseline walking time
  
- **Within-Person Variability:** SD(Slope) = `r round(as.numeric(random_effects["time", "StdDev"]), 1)` minutes/year
  - Individuals vary considerably in their rates of change over time
  
- **Intercept-Slope Correlation:** $r$ = `r round(as.numeric(random_effects["time", "Corr"]), 2)`
  - `r { { if (as.numeric(random_effects["time", "Corr"]) > 0) { "Positive correlation suggests that individuals with higher baseline walking time tend to show faster increases over time" } else { "Negative correlation suggests that individuals with higher baseline walking time tend to show slower increases (or greater decreases) over time" } } }`

<div class="technical-note">
**Prediction Methods:** We use the `marginaleffects` package to generate model-based predictions. This framework supports:

1. **Empirical-distribution predictions:** Predictions evaluated across the observed covariate distribution in the analytic sample
2. **Custom-grid predictions:** Predictions computed on scientifically meaningful values of key predictors (e.g., specific time points)
3. **Marginal predictions:** Predictions averaged over the distribution of nuisance covariates (when applicable)
4. **Counterfactual contrasts:** Predicted outcomes under hypothetical scenarios (e.g., setting sex to male vs female)

Unless otherwise stated, predictions are generated at the **population (fixed-effects) level**, with random effects set to zero, representing the expected outcome for an “average” individual conditional on the specified covariates.
</div>

```{r walk_bootstrap-sex-inference, eval=FALSE}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# FULL CHUNK — WALKING MODEL + BOOTSTRAP SEX DIFFERENCES
# Table W5
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(nlme)
library(marginaleffects)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# -----------------------------
# 1️⃣ Fit linear mixed model
# -----------------------------
m_main_walk <- lme(
  fixed = Walk_mins_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex,
  random = ~ time | id,
  data = df_mod,
  method = "REML",
  control = lmeControl(
    opt = "optim",
    maxIter = 100,
    msMaxIter = 100
  ),
  na.action = na.omit
)

# -----------------------------
# 2️⃣ Average predictions + bootstrap
# -----------------------------
avg_pred_sex_walk <- avg_predictions(
  m_main_walk,
  by = "sex",
  conf_level = 0.95
) %>%
  inferences(
    method = "boot",
    R = 1000   # use 1000 for publication-grade precision
  )

# -----------------------------
# 3️⃣ Display table (HTML/PDF)
# -----------------------------
kbl <- knitr::kable(
  avg_pred_sex_walk,
  caption = "**Table W5.** Average predicted daily walking time (min/day) by sex with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals",
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Sex", "Estimate (min/day)", "SE", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper")
)

if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  kbl %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
      full_width = FALSE,
      position = "center"
    )
} else {
  kbl %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      full_width = FALSE,
      position = "center"
    )
}

# -----------------------------
# 4️⃣ Word export (JAMA style)
# -----------------------------
jamatabs_style <- function(ft) {
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline_top(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- hline(ft, border = fp_border(width = 0.8), part = "header")
  ft <- hline_bottom(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 10, part = "all")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- valign(ft, valign = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding = 2, part = "all")
  ft <- autofit(ft)
  ft
}

fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  ifelse(is.na(x), NA_character_,
         formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = digits))
}

W5_df <- avg_pred_sex_walk %>%
  mutate(
    estimate = fmt_num(estimate, 1),
    std.error = fmt_num(std.error, 1),
    conf.low = fmt_num(conf.low, 1),
    conf.high = fmt_num(conf.high, 1)
  )

names(W5_df) <- c("Sex", "Estimate (min/day)", "SE", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper")

ft_W5 <- flextable(W5_df)
ft_W5 <- align(ft_W5, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
ft_W5 <- align(ft_W5, j = 2:5, align = "right", part = "all")
ft_W5 <- jamatabs_style(ft_W5)
ft_W5 <- set_caption(
  ft_W5,
  caption = "Table W5. Average predicted daily walking time (min/day) by sex with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals"
)

ft_W5 <- add_footer_lines(
  ft_W5,
  values = c(
    "Average marginal predictions by sex from a linear mixed-effects model.",
    "Model includes random intercept and random time slope by participant (id).",
    "Bootstrap confidence intervals computed with 100 resamples.",
    "REML estimation used."
  )
) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_W5 <- file.path(tab_dir, "Table_W5_avg_pred_sex_walking.docx")

doc_W5 <- read_docx()
doc_W5 <- body_add_par(doc_W5, "Table W5", style = "heading 1")
doc_W5 <- body_add_flextable(doc_W5, ft_W5)
print(doc_W5, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_W5)))

out_W5
```

<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Bootstrap Inference:** Non-parametric bootstrap resampling (e.g., R = 1,000 replications) provides robust confidence intervals that do not rely on asymptotic normality assumptions. This approach is particularly valuable when:

1. Sample sizes are moderate
2. Variance components are estimated with uncertainty (e.g., random intercepts and slopes)
3. Standard errors from asymptotic or delta-method approximations may be unreliable

Bootstrap intervals were computed by resampling participants (cluster bootstrap at the individual level) to preserve the within-person dependence structure of repeated measures.
</div>

# Sensitivity Analysis: Fixed-Effects Models

Fixed-effects (FE) models provide a complementary within-person perspective by controlling for all time-invariant individual characteristics—both measured and unmeasured. These models estimate effects using **only within-person variation**, eliminating confounding from stable individual differences.

# Sensitivity Analysis I: Fixed-Effects Models

Fixed-effects (FE) models provide a complementary **within-person** perspective by controlling for all **time-invariant** individual characteristics—both measured and unmeasured. These models estimate effects using **only within-person variation**, reducing bias from stable individual differences (e.g., long-standing health status, socioeconomic factors, habitual activity preferences).

<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Fixed-Effects Advantages:**

1. **Control of time-invariant confounding:** Automatically adjusts for all stable individual characteristics (observed or unobserved)
2. **Stronger within-person interpretation:** Estimates reflect how changes over time within the same person relate to changes in the outcome
3. **Robustness check:** Provides a useful benchmark against mixed-effects results that combine within- and between-person information

**Trade-offs:**

1. **Time-invariant predictors are not identified:** Sex and baseline age are absorbed by individual fixed effects and cannot be estimated directly
2. **Reduced efficiency:** Discards between-person information, often increasing uncertainty relative to mixed-effects models
3. **Sensitivity to measurement error:** Within-person differencing can amplify noise, potentially attenuating estimates
</div>



```{r walk_fe-data-prep}
## Data Preparation for FE Models
# Create within-person deviations
df_fe <- df_mod %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    # Within-person age deviation (time-varying component)
    age_w = age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Summary of within-person age variation
summary(df_fe$age_w)
```


<div class="technical-note">
**Within-Person Age Decomposition:**  
For fixed-effects models, age was decomposed into its **within-person (time-varying) component** by subtracting each individual’s mean age across observations:

\[
\text{age\_w}_{it} = \text{age}_{it} - \bar{\text{age}}_{i}
\]

This transformation isolates **within-person changes in age over time**, ensuring that fixed-effects estimates are identified exclusively from **intra-individual variation**. As a result, the corresponding coefficient reflects how changes in age within the same individual are associated with changes in the outcome, independent of all time-invariant characteristics.

The summary of \(\text{age\_w}\) confirms the presence of sufficient within-person age variation to support fixed-effects estimation.
</div>

## Linear FE Model

```{r walk_fe-linear, eval=TRUE}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# TABLE W6 — FIXED-EFFECTS (WITHIN-PERSON) MODEL (WALKING)
# Cluster-robust SE at individual level
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(fixest)
library(dplyr)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# Fit FE model
fe_linear_walk <- feols(
  Walk_mins_ponderada ~ time | id,
  data = df_fe,
  cluster = "id"
)

# Extract coefficient table safely
ct <- coeftable(fe_linear_walk)

beta  <- as.numeric(ct["time", "Estimate"])
se_b  <- as.numeric(ct["time", "Std. Error"])
p_val <- as.numeric(ct["time", "Pr(>|t|)"])

ci_low  <- beta - 1.96 * se_b
ci_high <- beta + 1.96 * se_b

# Sample sizes
n_obs <- nobs(fe_linear_walk)
n_id  <- length(unique(df_fe$id))

# Within R2 (safe extraction)
wr2 <- tryCatch(
  as.numeric(fitstat(fe_linear_walk, "wr2")),
  error = function(e) NA_real_
)

# Build table
table_W6 <- data.frame(
  Predictor = "Time (years)",
  `β (Estimate)` = sprintf("%.2f", beta),
  `Std. Error` = sprintf("%.2f", se_b),
  `Lower 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f", ci_low),
  `Upper 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f", ci_high),
  `p value` = ifelse(p_val < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_val)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Flextable
ft <- flextable(table_W6)
ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "all")
ft <- align(ft, j = 2:6, align = "right", part = "all")
ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
ft <- autofit(ft)

ft <- set_caption(
  ft,
  caption = "Table W6. Fixed-Effects (Within-Person) Linear Model for Daily Walking Time"
)

footer_text <- paste0(
  "Notes: β represents the within-person annual change in daily walking time (minutes/day). ",
  "Standard errors are cluster-robust at the individual level (id). ",
  "N (observations) = ", n_obs,
  "; N (individuals) = ", n_id,
  if (!is.na(wr2)) paste0("; Within R² = ", sprintf("%.3f", wr2), ".") else "."
)

ft <- add_footer_lines(ft, values = footer_text)
ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 9, part = "footer")
ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "footer")

# Export to Word
out_W6 <- file.path(tab_dir, "Table_W6_FE_within_walking.docx")

doc <- read_docx()
doc <- body_add_par(doc, "Table W6", style = "heading 1")
doc <- body_add_flextable(doc, ft)
print(doc, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_W6)))

out_W6
```

```{r walk_fe-vs-mixed-text, echo=FALSE}
mixed_time <- as.numeric(fixef(m_main_walk)["time"])
fe_time <- as.numeric(fe_time_coef)

aligned <- (sign(mixed_time) == sign(fe_time)) &&
  (abs(mixed_time) > 0) &&
  (abs(mixed_time - fe_time) / abs(mixed_time) < 0.20)

fe_vs_mixed_text <- if (aligned) {
  "The two estimates are closely aligned in both direction and magnitude, indicating that the observed temporal change is not driven by time-invariant individual characteristics. This concordance strengthens the interpretation of the time effect as a robust within-person phenomenon."
} else {
  "The difference between mixed-effects and fixed-effects estimates suggests that between-person differences or time-invariant characteristics may contribute to the observed association. In this context, the fixed-effects estimate represents the more conservative within-person effect."
}
```


```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide', eval=TRUE}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# TABLE W7 — FIXED-EFFECTS SPLINE MODEL (WALKING)
# Natural splines (df = 3)
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(fixest)
library(splines)
library(dplyr)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# 1️⃣ Fit FE spline model
fe_spline_walk <- feols(
  Walk_mins_ponderada ~ ns(time, df = 3) | id,
  data = df_fe,
  cluster = "id"
)

# 2️⃣ Extract coefficient table
ct <- coeftable(fe_spline_walk)

# Keep only spline terms
spline_terms <- grep("ns\\(time", rownames(ct), value = TRUE)

results <- data.frame(
  Predictor = paste("Spline basis", 1:length(spline_terms)),
  Beta = as.numeric(ct[spline_terms, "Estimate"]),
  SE = as.numeric(ct[spline_terms, "Std. Error"]),
  p = as.numeric(ct[spline_terms, "Pr(>|t|)"])
)

# Compute CI
results <- results %>%
  mutate(
    CI_low = Beta - 1.96 * SE,
    CI_high = Beta + 1.96 * SE
  )

# Sample info
n_obs <- nobs(fe_spline_walk)
n_id  <- length(unique(df_fe$id))

wr2 <- tryCatch(
  as.numeric(fitstat(fe_spline_walk, "wr2")),
  error = function(e) NA_real_
)

# Format numbers
table_W7 <- results %>%
  mutate(
    `β (Estimate)` = sprintf("%.2f", Beta),
    `Std. Error` = sprintf("%.2f", SE),
    `Lower 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f", CI_low),
    `Upper 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f", CI_high),
    `p value` = ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
  ) %>%
  select(
    Predictor,
    `β (Estimate)`,
    `Std. Error`,
    `Lower 95% CI`,
    `Upper 95% CI`,
    `p value`
  )

# 3️⃣ Flextable
ft <- flextable(table_W7)
ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "all")
ft <- align(ft, j = 2:6, align = "right", part = "all")
ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
ft <- autofit(ft)

ft <- set_caption(
  ft,
  caption = "Table W7. Fixed-Effects Spline Model for Daily Walking Time (Natural splines, df = 3)"
)

footer_text <- paste0(
  "Notes: Terms correspond to natural spline basis functions for time (df = 3) in a fixed-effects (within-person) model. ",
  "Individual spline coefficients are not directly interpretable; interpretation should rely on the predicted trajectory (Figure W1). ",
  "Standard errors are cluster-robust at the individual level (id). ",
  "N (observations) = ", n_obs,
  "; N (individuals) = ", n_id,
  if (!is.na(wr2)) paste0("; Within R² = ", sprintf("%.3f", wr2), ".") else "."
)

ft <- add_footer_lines(ft, values = footer_text)
ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 9, part = "footer")
ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "footer")

```{r walk_fe-spline-bootstrap, fig.cap="**Figure 8.** Within-person trajectory using natural splines with bootstrap 95% CI."}
## FE Spline Model with Bootstrap CIs — WALKING (Styled like Steps Figure)

library(fixest)
library(splines)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# -----------------------------
# 1️⃣ Fit FE spline model
# -----------------------------
fe_spline_walk <- feols(
  Walk_mins_ponderada ~ ns(time, df = 3) | id,
  data = df_fe,
  cluster = "id"
)

# -----------------------------
# 2️⃣ Fine grid for smooth curve
# -----------------------------
grid_spline <- data.frame(
  time = seq(min(df_fe$time, na.rm = TRUE),
             max(df_fe$time, na.rm = TRUE),
             length.out = 200)
)

X_spline <- model.matrix(~ ns(time, df = 3), data = grid_spline)

# Extract coefficients
b0_spline <- coef(fe_spline_walk)

b0_full <- setNames(rep(0, ncol(X_spline)), colnames(X_spline))
b0_full[names(b0_spline)] <- b0_spline

grid_spline$fit <- as.numeric(X_spline %*% b0_full)

# -----------------------------
# 3️⃣ Cluster bootstrap
# -----------------------------
set.seed(12345)
B <- 50  # Use 1000 for final version
ids <- unique(df_fe$id)
n_ids <- length(ids)

boot_spline <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = nrow(grid_spline), ncol = B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {

  sampled_ids <- sample(ids, size = n_ids, replace = TRUE)

  df_b <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(sampled_ids), function(k) {
    tmp <- df_fe %>% dplyr::filter(id == sampled_ids[k])
    tmp$idb <- paste0(as.character(sampled_ids[k]), "_", k)
    tmp
  }))

  mod_b <- feols(
    Walk_mins_ponderada ~ ns(time, df = 3) | idb,
    data = df_b,
    cluster = "idb"
  )

  bb <- coef(mod_b)

  bb_full <- setNames(rep(0, ncol(X_spline)), colnames(X_spline))
  bb_full[names(bb)] <- bb

  boot_spline[, b] <- as.numeric(X_spline %*% bb_full)
}

# Compute bootstrap CIs
grid_spline$ci_lower <- apply(boot_spline, 1, quantile, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
grid_spline$ci_upper <- apply(boot_spline, 1, quantile, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)

# -----------------------------
# 4️⃣ Plot (IDENTICAL STYLE TO STEPS FIGURE)
# -----------------------------
p_fe_spline_walk <- ggplot(grid_spline, aes(x = time, y = fit)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),
    fill = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", color = "black") +
  geom_line(
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, max(df_fe$time), by = 1)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::number_format(accuracy = 0.1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (years)",
    y = "Daily Walking Time (within-person estimate)",
    title = NULL,
    subtitle = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

print(p_fe_spline_walk)

# -----------------------------
# 5️⃣ Save figure
# -----------------------------
if (!exists("out_dir")) out_dir <- file.path(getwd(), "outputs")
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, "Figure_W1_FE_spline_bootstrap_walk_minutes.png"),
  plot = p_fe_spline_walk,
  width = 9,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

# Bayesian Hierarchical Models

Bayesian hierarchical models offer several advantages for longitudinal analysis of physical activity trajectories:

1. **Full uncertainty quantification:** Posterior distributions propagate uncertainty from all model components (fixed effects, random effects, and residual variance)
2. **Flexible prior specification:** Priors can incorporate weak regularization or substantive prior knowledge, improving stability in complex models
3. **Natural handling of hierarchical data:** Bayesian frameworks are well suited for repeated measures nested within individuals
4. **Probabilistic predictions:** Posterior predictive distributions allow direct inference on future or unobserved outcomes

## Model Specifications

We fitted three competing Bayesian hierarchical models to evaluate potential effect modification in longitudinal walking-time trajectories.

### Model 1: Additive Effects (Baseline Model)

$$
\text{WalkingMinutes}_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma)
$$

$$
\mu_{ij}
= \alpha
+ \beta_1 \,\text{Time}_{ij}
+ \beta_2 \,\text{Age}_{i}
+ \beta_3 \,\text{Sex}_{i}
+ b_{0i}
+ b_{1i}\,\text{Time}_{ij}
$$

*This baseline model specifies additive effects of time, baseline age, and sex on daily walking time, with individual-specific random intercepts and slopes.

---

### Model 2: Time × Sex Interaction

$$
\text{WalkingMinutes}_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma)
$$

$$
\mu_{ij}
= \alpha
+ \beta_1 \,\text{Time}_{ij}
+ \beta_2 \,\text{Sex}_{i}
+ \beta_3 \,(\text{Time}_{ij} \times \text{Sex}_{i})
+ \beta_4 \,\text{Age}_{i}
+ b_{0i}
+ b_{1i}\,\text{Time}_{ij}
$$

*This model allows the rate of change in walking time over time to differ by sex, testing for sex-specific longitudinal trajectories.

---

### Model 3: Time × Age Interaction

$$
\text{WalkingMinutes}_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma)
$$

$$
\mu_{ij}
= \alpha
+ \beta_1 \,\text{Time}_{ij}
+ \beta_2 \,\text{Age}_{i}
+ \beta_3 \,(\text{Time}_{ij} \times \text{Age}_{i})
+ \beta_4 \,\text{Sex}_{i}
+ b_{0i}
+ b_{1i}\,\text{Time}_{ij}
$$

*This model permits age-related heterogeneity in longitudinal walking-time trajectories by allowing the effect of time to vary as a function of baseline age.

<div class="statistical-rationale">
<strong>Bayesian Sensitivity Analysis (Model Fitting).</strong>  
To evaluate the robustness of the primary mixed-effects findings and to explore potential effect modification, we fitted Bayesian hierarchical models using <code>brms</code> (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo). Weakly informative priors were specified to stabilize estimation while remaining conservative with respect to effect sizes. 

Models were estimated with four chains (2,000 iterations each; 1,000 warm-up) and a target acceptance rate of <code>adapt_delta = 0.95</code> to reduce divergent transitions in hierarchical models. Convergence and sampling efficiency were assessed using standard diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample sizes, and trace plots). To improve reproducibility and reduce re-computation time, fitted models were saved to disk and the chunk was cached.
</div>



```{r walk_bayesian-models, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
## Model Fitting
## Priors on the outcome scale (walking minutes)
priors_walk <- c(
  prior(normal(85, 86), class = Intercept),
  prior(normal(0, 22), class = b),
  prior(exponential(0.023), class = sd),
  prior(exponential(0.023), class = sigma),
  prior(lkj(2), class = cor)
)

## Model 1: Additive effects
bayes_model_add_walk <- brm(
  formula = bf(Walk_mins_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time + sex + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod,
  family = gaussian(),
  #prior = priors_walk,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_add_walk")
)

## Model 2: Time × Sex interaction
bayes_model_time_sex_walk <- brm(
  formula = bf(Walk_mins_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time:sex + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod,
  family = gaussian(),
  #prior = priors_walk,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_time_sex_walk")
)

## Model 3: Time × Age interaction
bayes_model_time_age_walk <- brm(
  formula = bf(Walk_mins_ponderada ~ 1 + sex + time:age_c + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod,
  family = gaussian(),
  #prior = priors_walk,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_time_age_walk")
)

## Model 4: Skew-normal likelihood (robustness check)
bayes_model_skew_walk <- brm(
  formula = bf(Walk_mins_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time:sex + (1 + time | id)),
  data = df_mod,
  family = skew_normal(),
  #prior = priors_walk,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_skew_walk")
)
```

## Model Comparison

```{r walk_bayesian-comparison, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# TABLE W8 — Bayesian Model Comparison (LOO-CV)
# Outcome: Daily Walking Time
# ------------------------------------------------------------

library(loo)
library(dplyr)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# 1️⃣ Compute LOO for each model
loo_add_walk       <- loo(bayes_model_add_walk)
loo_time_sex_walk  <- loo(bayes_model_time_sex_walk)
loo_time_age_walk  <- loo(bayes_model_time_age_walk)
loo_skew_walk      <- loo(bayes_model_skew_walk)

# 2️⃣ Compare models
loo_comparison_walk <- loo_compare(
  loo_add_walk,
  loo_time_sex_walk,
  loo_time_age_walk,
  loo_skew_walk
)

loo_df_walk <- as.data.frame(loo_comparison_walk)
loo_df_walk$Model <- rownames(loo_df_walk)
rownames(loo_df_walk) <- NULL

# Reorder columns
loo_df_walk <- loo_df_walk %>%
  select(Model, elpd_diff, se_diff)

colnames(loo_df_walk) <- c(
  "Model",
  "ΔELPD",
  "SE (ΔELPD)"
)

# Format numbers
loo_df_walk$`ΔELPD` <- sprintf("%.2f", loo_df_walk$`ΔELPD`)
loo_df_walk$`SE (ΔELPD)` <- sprintf("%.2f", loo_df_walk$`SE (ΔELPD)`)

# 3️⃣ Create flextable
ft <- flextable(loo_df_walk)
ft <- align(ft, j = 1, align = "left", part = "all")
ft <- align(ft, j = 2:3, align = "right", part = "all")
ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
ft <- autofit(ft)

ft <- set_caption(
  ft,
  caption = "Table W8. Bayesian Model Comparison for Daily Walking Time Using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOO-CV)"
)

# Add footnote
ft <- add_footer_lines(
  ft,
  values = c(
    "Notes: Models compared using approximate Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation.",
    "ΔELPD represents the expected log predictive density difference relative to the best-fitting model (ΔELPD = 0).",
    "Higher ELPD indicates better predictive performance."
  )
)

ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 9, part = "footer")
ft <- align(ft, align = "left", part = "footer")

# 4️⃣ Export to Word
out_W8 <- file.path(tab_dir, "Table_W8_LOO_walk.docx")

doc <- read_docx()
doc <- body_add_par(doc, "Table W8", style = "heading 1")
doc <- body_add_flextable(doc, ft)
print(doc, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_W8)))

out_W8
```

<<div class="interpretation">
<strong>Bayesian model comparison (LOO-CV).</strong>  
Approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) suggested improved predictive
performance for the skew-normal hierarchical model relative to Gaussian
specifications (additive, time×sex, and time×age), with substantially higher
expected log predictive density (ΔELPD ≈ 286–289; SE ≈ 27).

However, PSIS diagnostics indicated a non-trivial number of influential observations
(Pareto-k > 0.7), suggesting potential instability of the LOO approximation.
Accordingly, LOO results are interpreted as indicative rather than definitive and
were complemented by posterior predictive checks and consistency of parameter
estimates across model families. Substantive conclusions regarding temporal trends
and effect modification were robust to the choice of likelihood.
</div>
<div class="technical-note">
<strong>Note on LOO diagnostics.</strong>  
A high proportion of Pareto-k values above 0.7 is not uncommon in hierarchical
longitudinal models with repeated measures. In such settings, LOO-CV remains useful
as a qualitative model comparison tool when interpreted alongside posterior
predictive checks and substantive robustness across model specifications.
</div>

```{r}
# comparison among all fitted models
main_data <- predictions(m_main_walk,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe1_data <- predictions(fe_linear_walk,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe2_data <- predictions(fe_spline_walk,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

bayes_data <- predictions(bayes_model_skew_walk,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

## predictions using the fitted Bayesian model incorporating full parameter uncertainty
bayes_pred_data <- datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1),
          model = bayes_model_skew_walk) %>%
  add_predicted_draws(bayes_model_skew_walk, 
                      ndraws = 500) %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(estimate = mean(.prediction),
            SD = sd(.prediction),
            conf.low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * SD,
            conf.high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * SD) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# data frame generation
main_data %>%
  mutate(model = "Base-case") %>%
  rbind(fe1_data %>% mutate(model = "FE linear sens")) %>% 
  rbind(fe2_data %>% mutate(model = "FE spline sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian regression sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian prediction\n(full uncertainty)")) %>% 
  mutate(time = rep(seq(0, 5, 1), times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>% as.data.frame()

# plot only showing mean predicted outcome
main_data %>%
  mutate(model = "Base-case") %>%
  rbind(fe1_data %>% mutate(model = "FE linear sens")) %>% 
  rbind(fe2_data %>% mutate(model = "FE spline sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian regression sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian prediction\n(full uncertainty)")) %>% 
  mutate(time = rep(seq(0, 5, 1), times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>% as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(aes(col = model), alpha = 1) +
  theme_dark() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Time (years)",
       y = "Predicted steps per day",
       col = "Models") +
  scale_color_tron()

# plot with uncertainty
main_data %>%
  mutate(model = "Base-case") %>%
  rbind(fe1_data %>% mutate(model = "FE linear sens")) %>% 
  rbind(fe2_data %>% mutate(model = "FE spline sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian regression sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian prediction\n(full uncertainty)")) %>% 
  mutate(time = rep(seq(0, 5, 1), times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>% as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(aes(col = model), alpha = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,

# Standardized residuals (Pearson)

# Residual plots

# Outcome 3: Peak 30-minute cadence (steps/min)


# Introduction

Physical activity is a critical determinant of health across the lifespan. Beyond overall volume and duration, **movement intensity** represents a key dimension of physical activity with important functional and prognostic implications. Accelerometry enables objective, continuous measurement of free-living movement, allowing the simultaneous assessment of multiple complementary activity metrics.

Peak 30-minute cadence, defined as the highest average stepping rate accumulated over any 30 minutes of the day, captures an intensity-related aspect of habitual activity that is closely linked to cardiorespiratory fitness and functional capacity. Understanding how this metric evolves over time—and whether trajectories differ across demographic groups—is essential for informing strategies aimed at preserving higher-intensity movement with ageing.

## Study Objectives

This analysis examines:

## Study Objectives

This analysis focuses on longitudinal changes in peak 30-minute cadence and examines:

1. **Temporal trends:** Within-person changes in peak 30-minute cadence (steps/min) over a 4-year observation period  
2. **Demographic differences:** Sex-specific trajectories adjusted for baseline age  
3. **Within-person dynamics:** Individual-level variability in baseline cadence and rates of change using mixed-effects modeling  
4. **Model validation:** Sensitivity analyses using frequentist methods to test the robustness of the base-case analysis (Bayesian regression model)


# Methods

## Data Structure and Preparation

<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Data Structure:** The analytic dataset comprises `r nrow(df)` observations from `r n_distinct(df$id)` unique participants assessed across `r n_distinct(df$wave)` measurement waves. Each row corresponds to a single person–wave observation, yielding a long-format longitudinal structure appropriate for hierarchical and within-person modelling approaches.
</div>

## Sample Selection


<div class="interpretation">
**Sample Retention:** The analysis includes `r nrow(df_acc)` valid accelerometry observations with non-missing peak 30-minute cadence values. Patterns of missingness and attrition were evaluated in sensitivity analyses to assess the potential for selection bias.
</div>

## Variable Construction


<div class="statistical-rationale">
**Outcome Definition:** Peak 30-minute cadence was operationalised as the maximum average stepping rate (steps/min) accumulated over any 30 minutes within a day, derived from raw accelerometry data and weighted to reflect population representativeness.

**Centering Rationale:** Baseline age was mean-centred (M = `r round(mean(df_mod$age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` years) to facilitate interpretation of the model intercept as the expected peak cadence at average age and baseline time. Centering improves numerical stability and reduces collinearity without altering slope estimates.
</div>
