# Sensitivity Analysis: Mixed-Effects Model

## Model Specification

The primary analytical model is a **linear mixed-effects model** with random intercepts and slopes:

$$
\text{Peak30}{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Time}{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Age}i + \beta_3 \text{Sex}i + b{0i} + b{1i}\text{Time}{ij} + \varepsilon{ij}
$$

Where:

- $\text{Peak30}_{ij}$ is the peak 30-minute cadence (steps/min) for individual $i$ at time $j$
- $\beta_0$ is the population-level intercept, representing expected peak cadence at baseline for a male participant of mean-centered age
- $\beta_1$ is the population-level linear effect of time (years since baseline)
- $\beta_2$ is the effect of baseline age (centered at the sample mean)
- $\beta_3$ represents the sex difference in peak cadence (reference category: Male)
- $b_{0i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{b_0})$ is the individual-specific random intercept
- $b_{1i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{b_1})$ is the individual-specific random slope for time
- $\varepsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ is the residual error term

<div class="statistical-rationale">
<strong>Model justification.</strong>
	1.	Random intercepts: Allow individuals to differ in baseline peak 30-minute cadence, capturing stable between-person differences in maximal habitual walking intensity.
	2.	Random slopes: Allow rates of change in peak cadence over time to vary across individuals, accommodating heterogeneity in longitudinal trajectories.
	3.	REML estimation: Restricted maximum likelihood was used to obtain unbiased estimates of variance components in the presence of unbalanced follow-up and unequal numbers of observations per participant.
	4.	Correlated random effects: The covariance between random intercepts and slopes was freely estimated, acknowledging that individuals with higher baseline cadence may experience different rates of change over time.
</div>
## Model Estimation

```{r peak30_main-model, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
## -----------------------------------------------------------
## Peak30 (steps/min): Mixed-effects model + Tables to Word
## Exports:
##   outputs/Table_C1_fixed_effects_peak30.docx
##   outputs/Table_C2_random_effects_peak30.docx
## -----------------------------------------------------------

library(nlme)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# Output folder
if (!exists("out_dir")) out_dir <- "outputs"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)

# -----------------------------
# Fit linear mixed-effects model
# -----------------------------
m_main_peak30 <- nlme::lme(
  fixed = CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex,
  random = ~ time | id,
  data = df_mod,
  method = "REML",
  control = nlme::lmeControl(
    opt = "optim",
    maxIter = 100,
    msMaxIter = 100
  ),
  na.action = na.omit
)

# -----------------------------
# JAMA-ish styling helpers
# -----------------------------
jamatabs_style <- function(ft) {
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline_top(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- hline(ft, border = fp_border(width = 0.8), part = "header")
  ft <- hline_bottom(ft, border = fp_border(width = 1.2), part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = 10, part = "all")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- valign(ft, valign = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- padding(ft, padding = 2, part = "all")
  ft <- autofit(ft)
  ft
}

fmt_p <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  out <- ifelse(is.na(x), NA_character_, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits))
  out[!is.na(x) & x < 0.001] <- "<0.001"
  out
}

# -----------------------------
# Table C1 — Fixed effects
# -----------------------------
fixed_effects <- summary(m_main_peak30)$tTable

C1_df <- as.data.frame(fixed_effects) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Parameter") %>%
  mutate(
    `95% CI Lower` = Value - 1.96 * Std.Error,
    `95% CI Upper` = Value + 1.96 * Std.Error
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    Parameter,
    Estimate = Value,
    SE = Std.Error,
    DF = as.integer(round(as.numeric(DF))),
    `t-value` = `t-value`,
    `95% CI Lower`,
    `95% CI Upper`,
    `p-value` = `p-value`
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Estimate = round(Estimate, 2),
    SE = round(SE, 2),
    `t-value` = round(`t-value`, 2),
    `95% CI Lower` = round(`95% CI Lower`, 2),
    `95% CI Upper` = round(`95% CI Upper`, 2),
    `p-value` = fmt_p(`p-value`, 3)
  )

ft_C1 <- flextable(C1_df) %>%
  align(j = 1, align = "left", part = "all") %>%
  align(j = 2:ncol(C1_df), align = "right", part = "all") %>%
  set_caption("Table C1. Fixed-effects estimates from the linear mixed-effects model (Peak 30-min cadence, steps/min).") %>%
  jamatabs_style() %>%
  add_footer_lines(values = c(
    "Notes: Linear mixed-effects model with random intercept and random time slope by participant (id).",
    "Fixed effects: time, centered baseline age (age_c), and sex.",
    "95% CIs computed as Estimate ± 1.96 × SE."
  )) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_C1 <- file.path(out_dir, "Table_C1_fixed_effects_peak30.docx")
doc_C1 <- read_docx() %>%
  body_add_par("Table C1", style = "heading 1") %>%
  body_add_flextable(ft_C1)
print(doc_C1, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_C1)))

# -----------------------------
# Table C2 — Random effects
# -----------------------------
vc <- nlme::VarCorr(m_main_peak30)

C2_df <- tibble(
  Component = c("Intercept SD", "Time slope SD", "Intercept–slope correlation", "Residual SD"),
  Estimate = c(
    as.numeric(vc["(Intercept)", "StdDev"]),
    as.numeric(vc["time", "StdDev"]),
    as.numeric(vc["time", "Corr"]),
    as.numeric(vc["Residual", "StdDev"])
  )
) %>%
  mutate(Estimate = round(Estimate, 3))

ft_C2 <- flextable(C2_df) %>%
  align(j = 1, align = "left", part = "all") %>%
  align(j = 2, align = "right", part = "all") %>%
  set_caption("Table C2. Random-effects variance components from the mixed-effects model (Peak 30-min cadence, steps/min).") %>%
  jamatabs_style() %>%
  add_footer_lines(values = c(
    "Notes: Variance components from the same linear mixed-effects model.",
    "Random effects structure: random intercept and random time slope by participant (id).",
    "SD indicates standard deviation."
  )) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_C2 <- file.path(out_dir, "Table_C2_random_effects_peak30.docx")
doc_C2 <- read_docx() %>%
  body_add_par("Table C2", style = "heading 1") %>%
  body_add_flextable(ft_C2)
print(doc_C2, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_C2)))

# Return paths (so you see them when knitting)
list(out_C1 = out_C1, out_C2 = out_C2)
```

<div class="interpretation">
<strong>Model Results Interpretation (Peak 30-min Cadence):</strong>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Time Effect:</strong> 
The population-average slope for time was −1.43 steps/min per year 
(95% CI: −1.77 to −1.08; <em>p</em> &lt; 0.001).
<br>
This indicates a clear longitudinal decline in peak 30-min cadence over the 4-year follow-up, after adjustment for age and sex.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Age Effect:</strong> 
Baseline age was negatively associated with peak cadence (β = −1.06 steps/min per additional year of age; 95% CI: −1.29 to −0.84; <em>p</em> &lt; 0.001).
<br>
Older participants exhibited systematically lower peak 30-min cadence levels across follow-up.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Sex Differences:</strong> 
Females accumulated on average 3.59 fewer steps/min during their peak 30-min period compared with males 
(95% CI: −5.92 to −1.27; <em>p</em> = 0.003), independent of age and time.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Between-Person Variability:</strong> 
There was substantial heterogeneity in baseline peak cadence 
(SD of random intercepts = 14.86 steps/min), indicating large individual differences in maximal walking intensity.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Within-Person Variability:</strong> 
Individuals also varied considerably in their rates of change over time 
(SD of random slopes = 2.43 steps/min per year), suggesting heterogeneous aging trajectories.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Intercept–Slope Association:</strong> 
The correlation between baseline level and rate of change was moderately negative (r = −0.27), indicating that individuals with higher initial peak cadence tended to experience steeper declines over time.
</li>
</ul>

</div>

```{r peak30_trajectories-age-sex, fig.cap="**Figure 6.** Predicted trajectories stratified by baseline age (±1 SD) and sex.", echo=FALSE}
## Predicted Trajectories by Age and Sex
# --- Ensure sex is a clean factor (Male/Female) ---
df_mod <- df_mod %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex = dplyr::case_when(
      sex %in% c("Male", "male", "M", "m") ~ "Male",
      sex %in% c("Female", "female", "F", "f") ~ "Female",
      as.character(sex) %in% c("1") ~ "Male",
      as.character(sex) %in% c("2") ~ "Female",
      TRUE ~ as.character(sex)
    ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Male", "Female"))
  )

# --- Age summaries (baseline scale for labels) ---
age_mean <- mean(df_mod$age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)
age_sd   <- sd(df_mod$age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)

# Prediction grid
grid_traj <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  time = seq(0, max(df_mod$time, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 100),
  age_c = c(-age_sd, 0, age_sd),
  sex = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = c("Male", "Female"))
)

# ---- Population-level predictions + 95% CI for fixed effects (manual) ----
# Design matrix must match the fixed-effects formula exactly:
X <- model.matrix(~ time + age_c + sex, data = grid_traj)

beta_hat <- nlme::fixef(m_main_peak30)
V_beta   <- vcov(m_main_peak30)

est <- as.numeric(X %*% beta_hat)
se  <- sqrt(diag(X %*% V_beta %*% t(X)))

pred_traj <- grid_traj %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    estimate  = est,
    conf.low  = est - 1.96 * se,
    conf.high = est + 1.96 * se
  )

# Age group labels
pred_traj <- pred_traj %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_group = dplyr::case_when(
      abs(age_c - (-age_sd)) < 1e-8 ~ paste0("Age: Mean - 1 SD (", round(age_mean - age_sd, 1), " yr)"),
      abs(age_c - 0)         < 1e-8 ~ paste0("Age: Mean (", round(age_mean, 1), " yr)"),
      abs(age_c - (age_sd))  < 1e-8 ~ paste0("Age: Mean + 1 SD (", round(age_mean + age_sd, 1), " yr)"),
      TRUE ~ "Age group"
    ),
    age_group = factor(
      age_group,
      levels = c(
        paste0("Age: Mean - 1 SD (", round(age_mean - age_sd, 1), " yr)"),
        paste0("Age: Mean (", round(age_mean, 1), " yr)"),
        paste0("Age: Mean + 1 SD (", round(age_mean + age_sd, 1), " yr)")
      )
    )
  )

# Plot (cadence range!)
p_trajectories <- ggplot2::ggplot(
  pred_traj,
  ggplot2::aes(x = time, y = estimate, color = sex, fill = sex, linetype = sex)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
    alpha = 0.18,
    color = NA
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 1.15) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ age_group, ncol = 3) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("Male" = "#ff9f43", "Female" = "#0abde3")) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values  = c("Male" = "#ff9f43", "Female" = "#0abde3")) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Male" = "solid", "Female" = "dashed")) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(30, 140),
    breaks = seq(30, 140, by = 10)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Time (years from baseline)",
    y = "Predicted Peak 30-min Cadence (steps/min)",
    color = "Sex",
    fill = "Sex",
    linetype = "Sex",
    title = "Predicted Trajectories by Age and Sex",
    subtitle = "Population-level predictions (fixed effects) with 95% confidence intervals"
  ) +
  theme_publication()

print(p_trajectories)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, "Figure_6_trajectories_age_sex_peak30.png"),
  plot = p_trajectories,
  width = 12,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

---

# Sensitivity Analysis: Fixed-Effects Models

Fixed-effects (FE) models provide a complementary within-person perspective on longitudinal change in peak 30-min cadence by controlling for all time-invariant individual characteristics—both measured and unmeasured. In contrast to mixed-effects models, FE models exploit only intra-individual variation over time, effectively removing between-person differences in baseline activity levels.

<div class="statistical-rationale">

**Rationale for Fixed-Effects Models:**

**Fixed-Effects Advantages:**

	1.	Control of time-invariant confounding: All stable individual characteristics (e.g., genetics, early-life factors, long-standing health status) are differenced out, even if unobserved.
	2.	Within-person interpretation: Estimated effects reflect how changes over time within the same individual are associated with changes in peak 30-min cadence.
	3.	Causal robustness: Under weaker assumptions than random-effects models, FE estimates can be interpreted as more robust evidence of within-person temporal change.

Limitations and Trade-offs:
	1.	Time-invariant covariates are not identifiable: Sex and baseline age effects are absorbed by individual fixed effects and cannot be estimated.
	2.	Reduced statistical efficiency: FE models discard between-person information, leading to wider confidence intervals compared with mixed-effects models.
	3.	Sensitivity to measurement error: Differencing over time may amplify noise in repeatedly measured outcomes.
</div>

## Data Preparation for FE Models

```{r peak30_fe-data-prep, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# Create within-person deviations (time-varying age)
df_fe <- df_mod %>%
  dplyr::group_by(id) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_w = as.numeric(age) - mean(as.numeric(age), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

# Summary of within-person age variation
summary(df_fe$age_w)
```

## Linear FE Model

```{r Table_C4_FE_linear_peak30, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## -----------------------------------------------------------
## Table C4 — Fixed-Effects (Within-Person) Linear Model
## Peak 30-min cadence (steps/min)
## Exports to: outputs/Table_C4_FE_linear_peak30.docx
## -----------------------------------------------------------

library(fixest)
library(broom)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(flextable)
library(officer)

# Ensure output directory exists
if (!exists("out_dir")) out_dir <- "outputs"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)

# IMPORTANT: build a clean FE dataset (prevents "variable names are limited..." errors)
df_fe_cad <- df_mod %>%
  transmute(
    id = id,
    time = time,
    CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada = CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada
  )

# Fit fixed-effects model (within-person)
fe_linear_cad <- feols(
  CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ time | id,
  data = df_fe_cad,
  cluster = "id"
)

# Table C4: time effect only
tab_C4 <- tidy(fe_linear_cad, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term == "time") %>%
  transmute(
    Predictor = "Time (years)",
    `β (Estimate)` = estimate,
    `Std. Error` = std.error,
    `Lower 95% CI` = conf.low,
    `Upper 95% CI` = conf.high,
    `p value` = p.value
  )

# ---- Table in report (kable) ----
knitr::kable(
  tab_C4,
  caption = "**Table C4.** Fixed-effects (within-person) linear model for Peak 30-min cadence (steps/min).",
  digits = 2
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )

# Model info for footnote
n_obs <- nobs(fe_linear_cad)
n_id  <- length(unique(df_fe_cad$id))
r2_within <- tryCatch(
  as.numeric(unlist(fixest::fitstat(fe_linear_cad, "wr2"))[1]),
  error = function(e) NA_real_
)

note_C4 <- paste0(
  "Notes: β represents the within-person annual change in peak 30-min cadence (steps/min). ",
  "Standard errors are cluster-robust at the individual level (id). ",
  "N (observations) = ", format(n_obs, big.mark = ","), "; ",
  "N (individuals) = ", format(n_id, big.mark = ","), ".",
  if (!is.na(r2_within)) paste0(" Within R² = ", round(r2_within, 3), ".") else ""
)

# ---- Export to Word ----
tab_word <- tab_C4 %>%
  mutate(
    `β (Estimate)` = sprintf("%.2f", `β (Estimate)`),
    `Std. Error`   = sprintf("%.2f", `Std. Error`),
    `Lower 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f", `Lower 95% CI`),
    `Upper 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f", `Upper 95% CI`),
    `p value`      = ifelse(`p value` < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", `p value`))
  )

ft_C4 <- flextable(tab_word) %>%
  bold(part = "header") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  set_caption("Table C4. Fixed-effects (within-person) linear model for Peak 30-min cadence (steps/min)") %>%
  add_footer_lines(note_C4) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_C4 <- file.path(out_dir, "Table_C4_FE_linear_peak30.docx")
doc_C4 <- read_docx() %>%
  body_add_par("Table C4", style = "heading 1") %>%
  body_add_flextable(ft_C4)

print(doc_C4, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_C4)))

# Also print the within-person effect text (optional)
fe_time_coef <- coef(fe_linear_cad)["time"]
fe_time_se   <- se(fe_linear_cad)["time"]

cat(
  "\n**Within-Person Time Effect (Fixed-Effects Model):**\n",
  "β_time =", round(fe_time_coef, 2), "steps/min per year\n",
  "SE =", round(fe_time_se, 2), "\n",
  "95% CI: [",
  round(fe_time_coef - 1.96 * fe_time_se, 2), ", ",
  round(fe_time_coef + 1.96 * fe_time_se, 2), "]\n"
)

out_C4
```

β<sub>time</sub> = <code>`r round(fixef(m_main_peak30)["time"], 2)`</code> steps/min per year</li>

<li><strong>Fixed-Effects Model Time Effect:</strong> 
β<sub>time</sub> = <code>`r round(fe_time_coef, 2)`</code> steps/min per year</li>
</ul>

<p>
<code>
`r {

This concordance strengthens the interpretation of the time effect as a robust within-person phenomenon."
  } else {
    "The divergence between mixed-effects and fixed-effects estimates suggests that time-invariant individual characteristics may contribute to the association. In this context, the fixed-effects estimate represents the more conservative within-person effect."
  }

</div>

```{r peak30_fe-spline-bootstrap, fig.cap="**Figure 8.** Within-person trajectory using natural splines with bootstrap 95% CI.", eval=FALSE}
## Spline FE Model with Bootstrap CIs
# FE spline model (within-person)
fe_spline_cad <- fixest::feols(
  CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ splines::ns(time, df = 3) | id,
  data = df_fe,
  cluster = "id"
)

# Grid
grid_spline <- data.frame(
  time = seq(min(df_fe$time, na.rm = TRUE), max(df_fe$time, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 200)
)

# IMPORTANT: for fixest predictions with FE present, we must provide an id.
# We'll use an arbitrary existing id and request predictions with FE excluded (xb only).
some_id <- as.character(df_fe$id[which(!is.na(df_fe$id))[1]])
grid_pred <- grid_spline
grid_pred$id <- some_id

# Point predictions (xb = TRUE gives linear predictor excluding fixed effects)
grid_spline$fit <- as.numeric(stats::predict(fe_spline_cad, newdata = grid_pred, type = "link", fixef = FALSE))

# Quick sanity checks
if (all(is.na(grid_spline$fit))) stop("All predictions are NA. Check that df_fe has valid time and outcome values.")
if (!("wave_num" %in% names(df_fe))) stop("df_fe$wave_num not found. Create wave_num before this chunk.")
min_wave <- min(df_fe$wave_num, na.rm = TRUE)
grid_spline$wave_num <- min_wave + grid_spline$time

# Bootstrap
set.seed(12345)
B <- 50
ids <- unique(df_fe$id)
n_ids <- length(ids)

boot_spline <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = nrow(grid_spline), ncol = B)

cat("Running bootstrap (", B, "iterations)...\n")

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  sampled_ids <- sample(ids, size = n_ids, replace = TRUE)

  df_b <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(sampled_ids), function(k) {
    tmp <- df_fe %>% dplyr::filter(id == sampled_ids[k])
    tmp$idb <- paste0(as.character(sampled_ids[k]), "_", k)
    tmp
  }))

  mod_b <- fixest::feols(
    CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ splines::ns(time, df = 3) | idb,
    data = df_b
  )

  # Predict on the same grid; need an idb in newdata
  some_idb <- as.character(df_b$idb[which(!is.na(df_b$idb))[1]])
  grid_pred_b <- grid_spline
  grid_pred_b$idb <- some_idb

  boot_spline[, b] <- as.numeric(stats::predict(mod_b, newdata = grid_pred_b, type = "link", fixef = FALSE))

  if (b %% 10 == 0) cat("  Completed", b, "iterations\n")
}

grid_spline$ci_lower <- apply(boot_spline, 1, stats::quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
grid_spline$ci_upper <- apply(boot_spline, 1, stats::quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)

# If everything is outside [30,140], don't hard-limit and let it autoscale
rng_all <- range(c(grid_spline$fit, grid_spline$ci_lower, grid_spline$ci_upper), na.rm = TRUE)

p_fe_spline <- ggplot2::ggplot(grid_spline, ggplot2::aes(x = wave_num, y = fit)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper), alpha = 0.30) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(df_fe$wave_num))) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(floor(rng_all[1]/5)*5, ceiling(rng_all[2]/5)*5, by = 5),
    limits = rng_all
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Measurement Wave",
    y = "Predicted Peak 30-min Cadence (steps/min) (Within-Person)",
    title = "Within-Person Longitudinal Trajectory (FE spline)",
    subtitle = "Natural splines (df = 3) with bootstrap 95% CI",
    caption = "Curve shows within-person change (FE), excluding individual fixed effects (xb only)."
  ) +
  theme_publication()

print(p_fe_spline)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, "Figure_8_FE_spline_bootstrap_peak30.png"),
  plot = p_fe_spline,
  width = 9,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

# Bayesian Hierarchical Models

Bayesian hierarchical models provide a complementary framework for longitudinal analysis of peak 30-minute cadence, offering several methodological advantages:
	1.	Full uncertainty quantification: Posterior distributions propagate uncertainty from fixed effects, random effects, and residual variance simultaneously.
	2.	Flexible prior specification: Weakly informative priors regularize estimation in complex hierarchical models and improve stability in unbalanced longitudinal designs.
	3.	Natural handling of multilevel data: Bayesian models explicitly reflect the nested structure of repeated observations within individuals.
	4.	Probabilistic interpretation: Posterior predictive distributions enable intuitive population-level and individual-level inference.

These models were used as sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of the frequentist mixed-effects findings and to explore potential effect modification.

##Model Specifications

We fit three Bayesian hierarchical models for peak 30-minute cadence (steps/min), differing in their fixed-effects structure while sharing a common random-effects specification.

Let Y_{ij} denote the peak 30-minute cadence (steps/min) for individual i at time point j.

⸻

Model 1: Additive Effects (Baseline Model)

$$
Y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma)
$$

$$
\mu_{ij}
= \alpha
	•	\beta_1 ,\text{Time}_{ij}
	•	\beta_2 ,\text{Age}_{i}
	•	\beta_3 ,\text{Sex}_{i}
	•	b_{0i}
	•	b_{1i},\text{Time}_{ij}
$$

This baseline model assumes additive population-level effects of time (years since baseline), baseline age (centered), and sex on peak 30-minute cadence. Individual-specific random intercepts and slopes allow both baseline cadence levels and rates of change over time to vary across participants.

⸻

Model 2: Time × Sex Interaction

$$
Y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma)
$$

$$
\mu_{ij}
= \alpha
	•	\beta_1 ,\text{Time}_{ij}
	•	\beta_2 ,\text{Sex}_{i}
	•	\beta_3 ,\text{Time}{ij} \times \text{Sex}{i}
	•	\beta_4 ,\text{Age}_{i}
	•	b_{0i}
	•	b_{1i},\text{Time}_{ij}
$$

This model evaluates whether longitudinal changes in peak 30-minute cadence differ by sex, allowing the slope of time to vary between males and females while retaining individual-level random effects.

⸻

Model 3: Time × Age Interaction

$$
Y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma)
$$

$$
\mu_{ij}
= \alpha
	•	\beta_1 ,\text{Time}_{ij}
	•	\beta_2 ,\text{Age}_{i}
	•	\beta_3 ,\text{Time}{ij} \times \text{Age}{i}
	•	\beta_4 ,\text{Sex}_{i}
	•	b_{0i}
	•	b_{1i},\text{Time}_{ij}
$$

This specification tests whether age modifies the rate of within-person change in peak 30-minute cadence, capturing potential acceleration or attenuation of decline with increasing baseline age.

<div class="statistical-rationale">
<strong>Bayesian Sensitivity Strategy.</strong>  
All Bayesian models share an identical random-effects structure (random intercepts and slopes for time), ensuring comparability across specifications. Differences in model performance therefore reflect alternative assumptions about effect modification rather than changes in hierarchical structure. These Bayesian analyses are interpreted as robustness checks and are not intended to replace the primary frequentist mixed-effects results.
</div>




```{r peak30_bayesian-models, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
## Model Fitting

# Bayesian hierarchical models for Peak 30-min cadence (steps/min)

# Common priors (cadence-scale)
priors_peak30 <- c(
  prior(normal(66, 20), class = Intercept),     # mean cadence around ~66 steps/min
  prior(normal(0, 5), class = b),              # slopes/effects typically a few steps/min
  prior(exponential(1), class = sd),           # random-effect SDs on cadence scale
  prior(exponential(1), class = sigma),        # residual SD on cadence scale
  prior(lkj(2), class = cor)                   # correlation of random effects
)

# Model 1: Additive effects
bayes_model_add_peak30 <- brms::brm(
  formula = brms::bf(
    CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time + sex + (1 + time | id)
  ),
  data = df_mod,
  family = gaussian(),
  #prior = priors_peak30,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_add_peak30")
)

# Model 2: Time × Sex interaction
# Use explicit main effects + interaction (avoid "time:sex" alone, which omits main effects)
bayes_model_time_sex_peak30 <- brms::brm(
  formula = brms::bf(
    CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time:sex + (1 + time | id)
  ),
  data = df_mod,
  family = gaussian(),
  #prior = priors_peak30,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_time_sex_peak30")
)

# Model 3: Time × Age interaction
# Use explicit main effects + interaction
bayes_model_time_age_peak30 <- brms::brm(
  formula = brms::bf(
    CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ 1 + sex + time:age_c + (1 + time | id)
  ),
  data = df_mod,
  family = gaussian(),
  #prior = priors_peak30,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_time_age_peak30")
)

# Model 4: Skew-normal distribution (robustness to mild skew)
bayes_model_skew_peak30 <- brms::brm(
  formula = brms::bf(
    CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ 1 + age_c + time:sex + (1 + time | id)
  ),
  data = df_mod,
  family = brms::skew_normal(),
  # prior = priors_peak30,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 12345,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  file = file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_skew_peak30")
)

# read saved models
bayes_model_add_peak30 <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_add_peak30.rds"))
```

## Model Comparison

```{r Table_C6_LOO_peak30, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## -----------------------------------------------------------
## Table C6 — Bayesian model comparison (LOO-CV)
## Peak 30-min cadence
## Exports to: outputs/Table_C6_LOO_peak30.docx
## -----------------------------------------------------------

library(loo)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(dplyr)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# Compute LOO
loo_add_peak30       <- loo(bayes_model_add_peak30)
loo_time_sex_peak30  <- loo(bayes_model_time_sex_peak30)
loo_time_age_peak30  <- loo(bayes_model_time_age_peak30)
loo_skew_peak30      <- loo(bayes_model_skew_peak30)

# Compare models
loo_comparison_peak30 <- loo_compare(
  loo_add_peak30,
  loo_time_sex_peak30,
  loo_time_age_peak30,
  loo_skew_peak30
)

# Convert to data frame
C6_df <- as.data.frame(loo_comparison_peak30) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Model") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), round, 2))

# ---- Print in Rmd ----
knitr::kable(
  C6_df,
  caption = "**Table C6.** Bayesian model comparison using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) for Peak 30-min cadence.",
  align = "l"
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )

# ---- Export to Word ----
if (!exists("out_dir")) out_dir <- "outputs"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir)

ft_C6 <- flextable(C6_df) %>%
  bold(part = "header") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  set_caption("Table C6. Bayesian model comparison using LOO-CV (Peak 30-min cadence)") %>%
  add_footer_lines(values = c(
    "Notes: Higher ELPD indicates better predictive performance.",
    "Values represent differences relative to the best-performing model."
  )) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_C6 <- file.path(out_dir, "Table_C6_LOO_peak30.docx")

doc_C6 <- read_docx() %>%
  body_add_par("Table C6", style = "heading 1") %>%
  body_add_flextable(ft_C6)

print(doc_C6, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_C6)))

out_C6
```
<div class="interpretation">
<strong>Bayesian Model Comparison (LOO-CV):</strong>

Leave-one-out cross-validation identified the <em>time × sex interaction model</em> as the best-supported specification (Δelpd = 0, reference model). Both the additive model (Δelpd = −2.9, SE = 3.7) and the time × age interaction model (Δelpd = −2.3, SE = 4.8) showed slightly lower expected out-of-sample predictive performance, with differences well within one standard error, indicating that these models are statistically indistinguishable from the best model in terms of predictive accuracy.

In contrast, the skew-normal model performed substantially worse (Δelpd = −10,424.2, SE = 51.9), providing no empirical support for departures from Gaussian residual assumptions in peak 30-min cadence. Overall, Bayesian model comparison suggests that allowing sex-specific temporal trajectories offers the most parsimonious improvement in predictive performance, although simpler additive formulations yield broadly comparable inferences.
</div>
<div class="statistical-rationale">
<strong>Interpretation of Δelpd:</strong> Differences in expected log predictive density (Δelpd) smaller than their associated standard errors indicate negligible evidence favoring one model over another. Large negative Δelpd values, as observed for the skew-normal model, reflect clear predictive inadequacy.
</div>

<div class="interpretation">
<strong>Posterior Predictive Assessment:</strong>

The posterior predictive check indicates good agreement between the observed distribution of peak 30-min cadence and data simulated from the fitted Bayesian model. The observed density (dark line) lies well within the range of posterior predictive distributions, suggesting that the model adequately captures both the central tendency and dispersion of the outcome. No systematic lack of fit or distributional misspecification is evident.
</div>

```{r peak30_compare-models, fig.cap="**Figure X.** Comparison of predicted Peak 30-min cadence trajectories across modelling approaches.", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# comparison among all fitted models
main_data_cad <- predictions(m_main_peak30,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe1_data_cad <- predictions(fe_linear_cad,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe2_data_cad <- predictions(fe_spline_cad,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

bayes_data_cad <- predictions(best_bayes_model_peak30,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

## predictions using the fitted Bayesian model incorporating full parameter uncertainty
bayes_pred_data_cad <- datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1),
          model = best_bayes_model_peak30) %>%
  add_predicted_draws(best_bayes_model_peak30, 
                      ndraws = 500) %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(estimate = mean(.prediction),
            SD = sd(.prediction),
            conf.low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * SD,
            conf.high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * SD) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

  rbind(bayes_data_cad %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian regression sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data_cad %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian prediction\n(full uncertainty)")) %>%

  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>% as.data.frame()

  rbind(fe2_data_cad %>% mutate(model = "FE spline sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_data_cad %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian regression sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data_cad %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian prediction\n(full uncertainty)")) %>% 
  mutate(time = rep(seq(0, 5, 1), times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>% as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(aes(col = model), alpha = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
                  ymax = conf.high, 
                  fill = model), alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  theme_dark() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.box = "vertical") +
  labs(x = "Time (years)",
       y = "Predicted Peak 30-min Cadence (steps/min)",
       col = "Models",
       fill = "Models") +
  scale_color_tron() +
  scale_fill_tron() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, 10),
                     limits = c(30, 90)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Optional export
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "Figure_compare_models_peak30_mean.png"), p_compare_mean, width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "Figure_compare_models_peak30_uncertainty.png"), p_compare_unc, width = 12, height = 6, dpi = 300)
## ------------------------------------------------------------
## Table C7 — Predicted Peak 30-min cadence across models (0–5 years)
## Exports to: outputs/Table_C7_predicted_peak30_model_comparison.docx
## ------------------------------------------------------------

library(marginaleffects)
library(tidybayes)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# Ensure output directory exists
if (!exists("out_dir")) out_dir <- "outputs"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)

times_grid <- 0:5

# Helper function
pred_ci <- function(model, times = 0:5) {
  predictions(model, newdata = datagrid(model = model, time = times)) %>%
    select(time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
}

# 1️⃣ Base-case mixed model
base_dat <- pred_ci(m_main_peak30, times_grid) %>%
  mutate(model = "Base-case")

# 2️⃣ FE linear
fe_lin_dat <- pred_ci(fe_linear_cad, times_grid) %>%
  mutate(model = "FE linear sens")

# 3️⃣ FE spline
fe_spl_dat <- pred_ci(fe_spline_cad, times_grid) %>%
  mutate(model = "FE spline sens")

# 4️⃣ Bayesian regression (posterior mean CI)
bayes_reg_dat <- pred_ci(best_bayes_model_peak30, times_grid) %>%
  mutate(model = "Bayesian regression sens")

# 5️⃣ Bayesian full uncertainty
bayes_full_dat <- datagrid(model = best_bayes_model_peak30, time = times_grid) %>%
  add_predicted_draws(best_bayes_model_peak30, ndraws = 500) %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(
    estimate = mean(.prediction),
    SD = sd(.prediction),
    conf.low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * SD,
    conf.high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * SD,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(model = "Bayesian prediction (full uncertainty)") %>%
  select(time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, model)

# Combine all
C7_long <- bind_rows(
  base_dat,
  fe_lin_dat,
  fe_spl_dat,
  bayes_reg_dat,
  bayes_full_dat
)

# Format values
C7_long <- C7_long %>%
  mutate(
    estimate = round(estimate, 1),
    conf.low = round(conf.low, 1),
    conf.high = round(conf.high, 1)
  )

# Convert to wide table
C7_wide <- C7_long %>%
  mutate(value = paste0(estimate, " [", conf.low, ", ", conf.high, "]")) %>%
  select(model, time, value) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = time, values_from = value, names_prefix = "t=")

# ---- Print in Rmd ----
knitr::kable(
  C7_wide,
  caption = "**Table C7.** Predicted peak 30-min cadence (steps/min) over time across primary and sensitivity models. Values are estimate [95% interval].",
  align = "l"
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center")

# ---- Export to Word ----
ft_C7 <- flextable(C7_wide) %>%
  bold(part = "header") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  set_caption("Table C7. Predicted peak 30-min cadence (steps/min) across models") %>%
  add_footer_lines(values = c(
    "Notes: Entries are model-based predictions at time t=0..5 years (estimate [95% interval]).",
    "Base-case = primary mixed-effects model; FE models = within-person fixed-effects;",
    "Bayesian regression sens = posterior mean-based; full uncertainty integrates posterior predictive draws."
  )) %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") %>%
  align(align = "left", part = "footer")

out_C7 <- file.path(out_dir, "Table_C7_predicted_peak30_model_comparison.docx")

doc_C7 <- read_docx() %>%
  body_add_par("Table C7", style = "heading 1") %>%
  body_add_flextable(ft_C7)

print(doc_C7, target = file.path(tab_dir, basename(out_C7)))

out_C7
```


# Appendix: Additional Analyses

## A1. Model Diagnostics
```{r}
# Standardized residuals
df_mod$resid <- residuals(m_main_peak30, type = "pearson")
df_mod$fitted <- fitted(m_main_peak30)

# Residuals vs fitted
p_resid1 <- ggplot(df_mod, aes(x = fitted, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(se = TRUE, color = "blue") +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted values",
    y = "Standardized residuals",
    title = "Residuals vs. fitted values"
  )

# Q-Q plot
p_resid2 <- ggplot(df_mod, aes(sample = resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Theoretical quantiles",
    y = "Sample quantiles",
    title = "Q–Q plot of residuals"
  )

# Residual distribution
p_resid3 <- ggplot(df_mod, aes(x = resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "Standardized residuals",
    y = "Frequency",
    title = "Distribution of residuals"
  )

# Combine plots
p_resid_combined <- p_resid1 / (p_resid2 | p_resid3)

print(p_resid_combined)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, "Figure_A1_diagnostics_peak30.png"),
  plot = p_resid_combined,
  width = 12,
  height = 10,
  dpi = 300
)
```


## A2. Random Effects Distribution

```{r peak30_random-effects-dist, fig.cap="**Figure A2.** Distribution of estimated random effects (BLUPs)."}
library(nlme)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# 1) BLUPs
ranef_df <- as.data.frame(ranef(m_main_peak30)) %>%
  dplyr::rename(
    Random_Intercept = `(Intercept)`,
    Random_Slope = time
  )

# 2) Correlación intercepto–pendiente (desde VarCorr)
vc_peak30 <- nlme::VarCorr(m_main_peak30)
corr_peak30 <- as.numeric(vc_peak30["time", "Corr"])

# 3) Plots
p_ranef1 <- ggplot(ranef_df, aes(x = Random_Intercept)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Random intercept (steps/min)", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Distribution of individual baseline deviations")

p_ranef2 <- ggplot(ranef_df, aes(x = Random_Slope)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Random slope (steps/min per year)", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Distribution of individual trajectory deviations")

p_ranef3 <- ggplot(ranef_df, aes(x = Random_Intercept, y = Random_Slope)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    x = "Random intercept (steps/min)",
    y = "Random slope (steps/min per year)",
    title = paste0("Correlation between random effects (r = ", round(corr_peak30, 2), ")")
  )

# 4) Combinar y FORZAR impresión
p_ranef_all <- (p_ranef1 | p_ranef2) / p_ranef3
print(p_ranef_all)

# 5) Guardar a archivo (evita depender del device de RStudio)
out_dir <- if (exists("out_dir")) out_dir else "outputs"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(out_dir, "Figure_A4_random_effects_peak30.png"),
  plot = p_ranef_all,
  width = 12,
  height = 10,
  dpi = 300
)
```

```{r peak30_individual-trajectories, fig.cap="**Figure A3.** Sample of individual trajectories (n=20) with population mean."}
# Random sample of individuals
```

# DG comments

Model selection should be detailed in the Methods' section. Something like: we compared several candidate models to identify the best-fitting specification for predicting the outcomes of interest (e.g., daily step count). Model comparison indicated that the model incorporating a sex-by-time interaction term with a skew-normal distributional family provided the best fit to the data (**Table X** *showing model fit parameters comparison*). The final model specification and prior distribution are detailed in the **Supplementary Material X**.

## Daily Steps

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
## ------------------------------------------------------------
## Daily Steps — Final Bayesian Model
## ------------------------------------------------------------

# Load final model (confirmed file name from outputs/)
bayes_steps <- readRDS(file.path("outputs", "bayes_model_beta_steps.rds"))

# ------------------------------------------------------------

plot_predictions(bayes_steps, by = "sex")

avg_predictions(bayes_steps, by = "sex", variables = list(time = 0))

avg_predictions(bayes_steps, by = "sex")

df_mod %>%

  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------

avg_predictions(
  bayes_steps,
  variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10))

avg_predictions(

  variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10)),

avg_predictions(

  variables = list(

)

library(metR)
library(cowplot)
library(patchwork)

predictions(
  bayes_steps,

  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    age = age_c + mean(df_mod$age),
    estimate = pmax(estimate, 0)
  ) %>%

  ) +

  ) +

    y = "Age",

```

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
sex_preds <- avg_predictions(bayes_steps, 
                             by = "sex", 
                             variables = list(time = 0)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```


At baseline (time = 0), males exhibited a higher predicted daily step count compared to females (males = `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/day, 95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 0)`; females = `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/day, 95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 0)`). These model-based predictions were consistent with the observed raw data means (males = 6,168 ± 3,502; females = 5,635 ± 3,207).

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
pred_sex <- avg_predictions(bayes_steps, by = "sex") %>% as.data.frame()
```


Average predicted daily steps, computed over the empirical distribution of covariates, were `r pred_sex %>% .[1, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/day (95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 0)`) for males, and `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/day (95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 0)`) for females (**Figure 1**). Sensitivity analyses using marginal means computed over a balanced grid of predictors yielded more similar estimates, suggesting smaller sex-specific differences on the predicted outcome when setting numeric predictors (i.e., time and age) at their means. *This approach is often used with randomized experiments when the analyst wishes to give equal weight to each combination of treatment conditions in the calculation of marginal means*.
 
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 1. Average predicted daily steps computed over (a) the empirical distribution of covariates, and (b) a balanced grid of covariates", eval=TRUE}
(plot_predictions(bayes_steps, by = "sex") +
  labs(x = "", y = "Predicted Steps", title = "Empirical grid of predictors") + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(5400, 6400), breaks = seq(0, 7000, 200))) + (plot_predictions(bayes_steps, by = "sex", newdata = "balanced") +
  labs(x = "", y = "Predicted Steps", title = "Balanced grid of predictors") + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(5400, 6400), breaks = seq(0, 7000, 200))) 
```

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
counterf_time <- avg_predictions(bayes_steps, variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10))) %>% as.data.frame()
```


Counterfactual predictions revealed a progressive decline in daily step count over time for the overall sample. Compared to baseline, average predicted steps declined by `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 3 years, `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 5 years, and `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 10 years.

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
time_sex_pred <- avg_predictions(bayes_steps, variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10)), by = c("time", "sex")) %>% as.data.frame()

# slopes
slopes <- avg_slopes(bayes_steps, 
           variables = "time", 
           by = "sex") %>% as.data.frame()
```

The rate of decline differed between males and females, as evidenced by the statistically credible sex-by-time interaction ($\beta_{males}$ = -189.97, 95% CrI -277.13 to -101.43; and $\beta_{females}$ = -239.61, 95% CrI -322.12 to -152.83). Averaging over the empirical distribution of covariates, males exhibited an annual decline of `r slopes %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 0)` steps/day per year (95% CrI `r slopes %>% .[1, 5] %>% round(., 0)` to `r slopes %>% .[1, 6] %>% round(., 0)`), whereas females declined at a rate of `r slopes %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 0)` steps/day per year (95% CrI `r slopes %>% .[2, 5] %>% round(., 0)` to `r slopes %>% .[2, 6] %>% round(., 0)`). Specifically, at 3 years, males showed a `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) reduction from baseline compared to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) for females; at 5 years, reductions were `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%), and `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%), respectively; and at 10 years, males showed a `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) decline compared to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) for females. 

**Figure X** presents predicted daily step counts as a function of time and age, stratified by sex. Both panels reveal a clear gradient, with higher step counts observed among younger participants at earlier time points and progressively lower counts with advancing age and follow-up duration. The steeper decline among females is visually apparent in the contour patterns, with isoclines shifting more rapidly across the time axis compared to males.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure X. Predicted daily step counts adjusted for time, age, and sex", fig.height=7, fig.width=9, eval=TRUE}
# libraries
library(metR)
library(cowplot)
library(patchwork)

# plot
predictions(bayes_steps, 
            newdata = datagrid(
              time = seq(0, 10, by = 1),
              age_c = seq(min(df_mod$age_c), max(df_mod$age_c), by = 1),  
              sex = c("Male", "Female")
            )) %>%
  mutate(age = age_c + mean(df_mod$age),
         estimate = ifelse(estimate <= 0, 0, estimate)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(time, age, fill = estimate, group = sex)) +
  geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +
  geom_contour2(aes(x = time, y = age, z = estimate), col = "black",
                breaks = seq(0, 7000, 1000)) +
  geom_text_contour(aes(z = estimate), stroke = 0.05, size = 4.5, skip = 0,
                    label.placer = label_placer_n(1), min.size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  # geom_line(data = tidy_epred %>%
  # filter(round(.epred, 4) == -0.5), aes(x = dose_by_100, y = baseline_glyc), col = "red") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = colorspace::heat_hcl(7)) + # another option is scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma")
  theme_tidybayes() +
  panel_border() +
  labs(x = "Time (years)",
       y = "Age",
       fill = "Predicted\nsteps") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 120, 5)) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
final_pred <- avg_predictions(bayes_steps, variables = list(time = c(0, 10), age_c = c(70 - mean(df_mod$age), 85 - mean(df_mod$age))), by = c("age_c", "time")) %>% as.data.frame()
```


Notably, the age-related gradient in physical activity was evident across all time points, indicating that both chronological aging and time-dependent decline contribute independently to reductions in daily step count. For instance, a 70-year-old individual at baseline was predicted to accumulate approximately `r round(final_pred[1, 3], 0)` steps/day (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[1, 4], 0)` to `r round(final_pred[1, 5], 0)`), declining to `r round(final_pred[2, 3], 0)` steps/day after 10 years (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[2, 4], 0)` to `r round(final_pred[2, 5], 0)`). In contrast, an 85-year-old at baseline was predicted to take `r round(final_pred[3, 3], 0)` steps/day (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[3, 4], 0)` to `r round(final_pred[3, 5], 0)`), with a 10-year projection of `r round(final_pred[4, 3], 0)` steps/day (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[4, 4], 0)` to `r round(final_pred[4, 5], 0)`).

### Sensitivity Analysis

Predicted values of daily step counts at each time point (0 to 5 years) are presented in **Table X**. Across all model specifications, point estimates were highly consistent, with predicted baseline values ranging from *5,137 to 6,707* steps/day, and 5-year predictions ranging from *3,447 to 4,697* steps/day. The direction and magnitude of temporal decline were concordant across approaches, supporting the robustness of our primary findings.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# comparison among all fitted models
main_data <- predictions(m_main_steps,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe1_data <- predictions(fe_linear,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe2_data <- predictions(fe_spline,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

bayes_data <- predictions(bayes_steps,
            newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 5, 1))) %>% select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

## predictions using the fitted Bayesian model incorporating full parameter uncertainty

          model = bayes_steps) %>%
  add_predicted_draws(bayes_steps, 
                      ndraws = 500) %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(estimate = mean(.prediction),
            SD = sd(.prediction),
            conf.low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * SD,
            conf.high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * SD) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# data frame generation
result_data <- main_data %>%
  mutate(model = "Base-case") %>%

  rbind(bayes_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian regression sens")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian prediction\n(full uncertainty)")) %>% 
  mutate(time = rep(seq(0, 5, 1), times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 0) %>%
  as.data.frame()

  rbind(bayes_pred_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian model\n(posterior predictions)")) %>% 
  mutate(time = rep(seq(0, 5, 1), times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>% as.data.frame() %>%

# plot with uncertainty

  rbind(bayes_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian model\n(expectation of the posterior)")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian model\n(posterior predictions)")) %>% 
  mutate(time = rep(seq(0, 5, 1), times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>% as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(aes(col = model), alpha = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
```

Uncertainty intervals were narrowest for the fixed-effects models and widest for the Bayesian posteriors estimates, which incorporate residual variability (i.e., *expectation of the posterior*) in addition to parameter uncertainty (i.e., *posterior predictions*). Bayesian regression models yielded larger interval widths, reflecting an increase of coefficient uncertainty. The non-linear models (Bayesian and spline-based models) produced similar trajectories compared to the linear specifications, suggesting that the linear assumption was reasonable, with modest nonlinearity presence, which does not substantively alter conclusions.

## Daily Walking Time

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# model
bayes_model_beta_walk <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "bayes_model_skew_walk.rds"))

# preds
sex_preds <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_beta_walk, by = "sex", variables = list(time = 0)) %>% as.data.frame()
```


At baseline (time = 0), males exhibited a higher predicted daily walking time compared to females (males = `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 2] %>% round(., 0)` min/day, 95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 0)`; females = `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 2] %>% round(., 0)` min/day, 95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 0)`). These model-based predictions were consistent with the observed raw data means (males = 90.20 ± 44.90; females = 80.80 ± 41.40).

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
pred_sex <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_beta_walk, by = "sex") %>% as.data.frame()
```


Average predicted daily walking time, computed over the empirical distribution of covariates, was `r pred_sex %>% .[1, 2] %>% round(., 0)` min/day (95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 0)`) for males, and `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 2] %>% round(., 0)` min/day (95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 0)`) for females (**Figure 1**). Sensitivity analyses using marginal means computed over a balanced grid of predictors yielded more similar estimates, suggesting smaller sex-specific differences in predicted walking time when setting numeric predictors (i.e., time and age) at their means.
 
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 1. Average predicted daily steps computed over (a) the empirical distribution of covariates, and (b) a balanced grid of covariates", eval=TRUE}
(plot_predictions(bayes_model_beta_walk, by = "sex") +
  labs(
    x = "",
    y = "Predicted Daily Walking Time (min/day)",
    title = "Empirical grid of predictors"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(80, 95),
    breaks = seq(80, 95, 2)
  )) +

(plot_predictions(bayes_model_beta_walk, by = "sex", newdata = "balanced") +
  labs(
    x = "",
    y = "Predicted Daily Walking Time (min/day)",
    title = "Balanced grid of predictors"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(80, 95),
    breaks = seq(80, 95, 2)
  ))
```

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
counterf_time <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_beta_walk, variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10))) %>% as.data.frame()
```


Counterfactual predictions revealed a progressive decline in daily walking time over time for the overall sample. Compared to baseline, average predicted walking time declined by `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 3 years, `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 5 years, and `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 10 years.

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
time_sex_pred <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_beta_walk, variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10)), by = c("time", "sex")) %>% as.data.frame()

# slopes
slopes <- avg_slopes(bayes_model_beta_walk, 
           variables = "time", 
           by = "sex") %>% as.data.frame()
```

The rate of decline differed between males and females, as evidenced by the statistically credible sex-by-time interaction ($\beta_{males}$ = -2.31, 95% CrI -3.53 to -1.14; and $\beta_{females}$ = -2.90, 95% CrI -4.05 to -1.78). Averaging over the empirical distribution of covariates, males exhibited an annual decline of `r slopes %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 2)` min/day per year (95% CrI `r slopes %>% .[1, 5] %>% round(., 2)` to `r slopes %>% .[1, 6] %>% round(., 2)`), whereas females declined at a rate of `r slopes %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 2)` min/day per year (95% CrI `r slopes %>% .[2, 5] %>% round(., 2)` to `r slopes %>% .[2, 6] %>% round(., 2)`). Specifically, at 3 years, males showed a `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) reduction from baseline compared to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) for females; at 5 years, reductions were `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%), and `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%), respectively; and at 10 years, males showed a `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) decline compared to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) for females. 

**Figure X** presents predicted daily walking time as a function of time and age, stratified by sex. Both panels reveal a clear gradient, with higher daily walking time observed among younger participants at earlier time points and progressively lower walking time with advancing age and follow-up duration. The steeper decline among females is visually apparent in the contour patterns, with isoclines shifting more rapidly across the time axis compared to males.


```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
  mutate(Time = seq(0, 5, 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(`F-E spline OLS model` = paste0(round(estimate, 0), " (", round(conf.low, 0), " to ", round(conf.high, 0), ")")) %>%
  select(`F-E spline OLS model`)) %>%
  
  # linear predictions from Bayesian model
  cbind(bayes_data %>%
  mutate(Time = seq(0, 5, 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(`Bayesian model` = paste0(round(estimate, 0), " (", round(conf.low, 0), " to ", round(conf.high, 0), ")")) %>%
  select(`Bayesian model`)) %>%
  
  # full-uncertainty from Bayesian model
  cbind(bayes_pred_data %>%
  mutate(Time = seq(0, 5, 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(`Bayesian model (full uncertainty)` = paste0(round(estimate, 0), " (", round(conf.low, 0), " to ", round(conf.high, 0), ")")) %>%
  select(`Bayesian model (full uncertainty)`)) %>%
  
  # formatting
  kable(
  .,
  caption = "**Table X.** Model predictions",
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )
```

Uncertainty intervals were narrowest for the fixed-effects models and widest for the Bayesian posteriors estimates, which incorporate residual variability (i.e., *expectation of the posterior*) in addition to parameter uncertainty (i.e., *posterior predictions*). Bayesian regression models yielded larger interval widths, reflecting an increase of coefficient uncertainty. The non-linear models (Bayesian and spline-based models) produced similar trajectories compared to the linear specifications, suggesting that the linear assumption was reasonable, with modest nonlinearity presence, which does not substantively alter conclusions.

## Peak 30-Minute Walking Cadence

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
sex_preds <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30, by = "sex", variables = list(time = 0)) %>% as.data.frame()
```


At baseline (time = 0), males exhibited a higher predicted peak 30-min cadence compared to females (males = `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/min, 95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 0)`; females = `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/min, 95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 0)`). These model-based predictions were consistent with the observed raw data means (males = 68.80 ± 16.40; females = 63.90 ± 16.30).

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
pred_sex <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30, by = "sex") %>% as.data.frame()
```


Average predicted peak 30-min cadence, computed over the empirical distribution of covariates, was `r pred_sex %>% .[1, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/min (95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 0)`) for males, and `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 2] %>% round(., 0)` steps/min (95% CrI `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 3] %>% round(., 0)` to `r sex_preds %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 0)`) for females (**Figure 1**). Sensitivity analyses using marginal means computed over a balanced grid of predictors yielded more similar estimates, suggesting smaller sex-specific differences in predicted peak 30-min cadence when setting numeric predictors (i.e., time and age) at their means.
 
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 1. Average predicted daily steps computed over (a) the empirical distribution of covariates, and (b) a balanced grid of covariates", eval=TRUE}
(plot_predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30, by = "sex") +
  labs(x = "", y = "Predicted Steps", title = "Empirical grid of predictors") + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(60, 75), breaks = seq(0, 100, 5))) + (plot_predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30, by = "sex", newdata = "balanced") +
  labs(x = "", y = "Predicted Steps", title = "Balanced grid of predictors") + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(60, 75), breaks = seq(0, 100, 5))) 
```

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
counterf_time <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30, variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10))) %>% as.data.frame()
```


Counterfactual predictions revealed a progressive decline in peak 30-min cadence over time for the overall sample. Compared to baseline, average predicted peak 30-min cadence declined by `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[2, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 3 years, `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[3, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 5 years, and `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 2] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 4] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (counterf_time %>% .[4, 3] / counterf_time %>% .[1, 2])) * 100, 2)`%) at 10 years.

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
time_sex_pred <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30, variables = list(time = c(0, 3, 5, 10)), by = c("time", "sex")) %>% as.data.frame()

# slopes
slopes <- avg_slopes(bayes_model_skew_peak30, 
           variables = "time", 
           by = "sex") %>% as.data.frame()
```

The rate of decline differed between males and females, as evidenced by the statistically credible sex-by-time interaction ($\beta_{males}$ = -1.10, 95% CrI -1.60 to -0.60; and $\beta_{females}$ = -1.63, 95% CrI -2.10 to -1.17). Averaging over the empirical distribution of covariates, males exhibited an annual decline of `r slopes %>% .[1, 4] %>% round(., 2)` steps/min per year (95% CrI `r slopes %>% .[1, 5] %>% round(., 2)` to `r slopes %>% .[1, 6] %>% round(., 2)`), whereas females declined at a rate of `r slopes %>% .[2, 4] %>% round(., 2)` steps/min per year (95% CrI `r slopes %>% .[2, 5] %>% round(., 2)` to `r slopes %>% .[2, 6] %>% round(., 2)`). Specifically, at 3 years, males showed a `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[3, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) reduction from baseline compared to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[4, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) for females; at 5 years, reductions were `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[5, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%), and `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[6, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%), respectively; and at 10 years, males showed a `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[7, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[1, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) decline compared to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 3] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% (95% CrI `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 5] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`% to `r round((1 - (time_sex_pred %>% .[8, 4] / time_sex_pred %>% .[2, 3])) * 100, 2)`%) for females. 

**Figure X** presents predicted peak 30-min cadence as a function of time and age, stratified by sex. Both panels reveal a clear gradient, with higher peak 30-min cadence observed among younger participants at earlier time points and progressively lower peak 30-min cadence with advancing age and follow-up duration. The steeper decline among females is visually apparent in the contour patterns, with isoclines shifting more rapidly across the time axis compared to males.

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
final_pred <- avg_predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30, variables = list(time = c(0, 10), age_c = c(70 - mean(df_mod$age), 85 - mean(df_mod$age))), by = c("age_c", "time")) %>% as.data.frame()
```

Notably, the age-related gradient in peak 30-min cadence was evident across all time points, indicating that both chronological aging and time-dependent decline contribute independently to reductions in walking intensity. For instance, a 70-year-old individual at baseline was predicted to achieve a peak 30-min cadence of approximately `r round(final_pred[1, 3], 2)` steps/min (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[1, 4], 2)` to `r round(final_pred[1, 5], 2)`), declining to `r round(final_pred[2, 3], 2)` steps/min after 10 years (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[2, 4], 2)` to `r round(final_pred[2, 5], 2)`). In contrast, an 85-year-old at baseline was predicted to achieve `r round(final_pred[3, 3], 2)` steps/min (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[3, 4], 2)` to `r round(final_pred[3, 5], 2)`), with a 10-year projection of `r round(final_pred[4, 3], 2)` steps/min (95% CrI `r round(final_pred[4, 4], 2)` to `r round(final_pred[4, 5], 2)`).

### Sensitivity Analysis

Predicted values of peak 30-min cadence at each time point (0 to 5 years) are presented in **Table X**. Across all model specifications, point estimates were highly consistent, with predicted baseline values ranging from *65 to 73* steps/min, and 5-year predictions ranging from *55 to 60* steps/min. The direction and magnitude of temporal decline were concordant across approaches, supporting the robustness of our primary findings.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Peak 30-min cadence: Model comparison (0–5 years)
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Predictions from all models
main_data <- predictions(m_main_peak30,
            newdata = datagrid(time = 0:5)) %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe1_data <- predictions(fe_linear_cad,
            newdata = datagrid(time = 0:5)) %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

fe2_data <- predictions(fe_spline_cad,
            newdata = datagrid(time = 0:5)) %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

bayes_data <- predictions(bayes_model_skew_peak30,
            newdata = datagrid(time = 0:5)) %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# Bayesian full posterior predictive uncertainty
bayes_pred_data <- datagrid(time = 0:5,
          model = bayes_model_skew_peak30) %>%
  add_predicted_draws(bayes_model_skew_peak30, ndraws = 500) %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(
    estimate = mean(.prediction),
    SD = sd(.prediction),
    conf.low = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * SD,
    conf.high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * SD
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Mean trajectory comparison plot
# ------------------------------------------------------------

exp_plot <- main_data %>%
  mutate(model = "Linear-mixed model") %>%
  rbind(fe1_data %>% mutate(model = "FE linear OLS model")) %>%
  rbind(fe2_data %>% mutate(model = "FE spline OLS model")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian model (posterior mean)")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_pred_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian model (posterior prediction)")) %>%
  mutate(time = rep(0:5, times = 5)) %>%
  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(aes(col = model), linewidth = 1) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    x = "Time (years)",
    y = "Predicted peak 30-min cadence (steps/min)",
    col = "Models"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(40, 90, 5))

exp_plot

# ------------------------------------------------------------

unc_plot <- main_data %>%
  mutate(model = "Linear-mixed model") %>%
  rbind(fe1_data %>% mutate(model = "FE linear OLS model")) %>%
  rbind(fe2_data %>% mutate(model = "FE spline OLS model")) %>%
  rbind(bayes_data %>% mutate(model = "Bayesian model (posterior mean)")) %>%

  select(model, time, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(aes(col = model), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
                  ymax = conf.high,
                  fill = model),
              alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Time (years)",
    y = "Predicted peak 30-min cadence (steps/min)",
    col = "Models",
```

Uncertainty intervals were narrowest for the fixed-effects models and widest for the Bayesian posteriors estimates, which incorporate residual variability (i.e., *expectation of the posterior*) in addition to parameter uncertainty (i.e., *posterior predictions*). Bayesian regression models yielded larger interval widths, reflecting an increase of coefficient uncertainty. ```

To contextualize our findings, we compared model-based predictions with published [normative reference values](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30676186/) for peak 30-min cadence in older adults (**Figure X**). Predicted cadence values for both males and females in our sample fell near the age- and sex-specific normative median. Over the 10-year follow-up period, predicted values declined comparably relative to normative aging trajectories, with 32 males and 16 women showed predicted values falling below the 25th percentile by year 5. This pattern suggests that our cohort's trajectory is consistent with population-level aging patterns.


```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Evoluation across time of a 70-year average person in our sample population"}
# Digitized normative quantiles for Peak 30-min Cadence (steps/min)
# Source: Aguiar et al. (2019) -> "Normative Peak 30-Min Cadence (Steps per Minute) Values for Older Adults: NHANES 2005-2006"
normative_cadence <- data.frame(
  age = c(60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84, 85),
  
  # Men (solid lines)
  men_p5  = c(44, 45, 46, 47, 47, 48, 48, 48, 48, 48, 47, 46, 45, 44, 42, 40, 38, 36, 33, 30, 28, 26, 24, 22, 20, 18),
  men_p25 = c(59, 60, 61, 62, 62, 63, 63, 63, 63, 62, 61, 60, 58, 56, 54, 52, 49, 46, 43, 40, 37, 34, 31, 28, 26, 24),
  men_p50 = c(71, 72, 73, 74, 74, 75, 75, 75, 75, 74, 73, 72, 70, 68, 66, 63, 60, 57, 53, 50, 46, 43, 40, 37, 34, 32),
  
  # Women (dashed lines)
  women_p5  = c(32, 33, 34, 35, 35, 36, 36, 36, 36, 35, 35, 34, 33, 32, 30, 29, 27, 25, 23, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15),
  women_p25 = c(50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 54, 55, 55, 55, 54, 54, 53, 51, 49, 47, 45, 43, 40, 37, 35, 33, 31, 29, 27, 25, 24),
  women_p50 = c(64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 68, 69, 69, 69, 68, 67, 66, 64, 62, 60, 57, 54, 51, 48, 45, 42, 40, 38, 36, 34, 32)
)


# predictions
pred_data <- predictions(
  bayes_model_skew_peak30, newdata = datagrid(time = seq(0, 15), age_c = 70 - mean(df_mod$age), sex = c("Male", "Female"))) %>%
  posterior_draws() %>%
  mutate(age = age_c + mean(df_mod$age) + time) %>%
  # data at baseline
  #filter(time == 0) %>%
  select(age, sex, time, draw) %>% 
  group_by(age, sex) %>%
  summarise(mean_cad = mean(draw),
            lower = mean_cad - qnorm(0.975) * sd(draw),
            upper = mean_cad + qnorm(0.975) * sd(draw)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  as.data.frame()


# Join predictions with normative medians
pred_data %>%
  mutate(lower = ifelse(lower < 0, 0, lower)) %>%
  #filter(age >= 70 & age <= 85) %>%
  #filter(sex == "Female") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = mean_cad)) +
  geom_pointinterval(aes(ymin = lower, 
                         ymax = upper, 
             group = sex, 
             col = sex),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_line(data = normative_cadence %>%
  filter(age >= 70 & age <= 85),
            aes(y = women_p50),
            linetype = 2,
            col = "purple4",
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = normative_cadence %>%
  filter(age >= 70 & age <= 85),
            aes(y = men_p50),
            linetype = 2,
            col = "orange4",
            linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("orange", "purple")) +
  labs(y = "Predicted peak 30-min cadence (steps/min)",
       x = "Age",
       subtitle = "Brown and dark-purple dashed lines represent 50th percentile normative intensity values",
       col = "Sex",
       title = "Evolution across time of an average person")
```
