<!-- =================================================================== -->

# Revision

This section contains the additional analyses requested during peer review. Each
subsection is labelled with the corresponding reviewer question (R1 = Reviewer 1,
R2 = Reviewer 2) and is designed to be read alongside the itemized
*Response to Reviewers*. All analyses reuse the primary analytic object `df_mod`
(2,030 person–wave observations from 644 participants). To keep this section
self-contained, we first (re)derive a small number of helper variables.

```{r rev-setup, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(lme4); library(ggplot2)
})

# Helper variables used across the revision analyses -------------------------
df_rev <- df_mod %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    first_wave   = min(wave_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_wave    = max(wave_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_waves_i    = dplyr::n()
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    # Attained (chronological) age at each wave, mean-centred on baseline age
    age_attained_c = as.numeric(age - mean(age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)),
    # Survey weights rescaled to mean 1 (preserves relative weighting, avoids
    # numerical scaling warnings from the raw expansion weights)
    w_norm = weights_nhats / mean(weights_nhats, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

outcomes <- c(
  Steps   = "Steps_ponderada",
  Walk    = "Walk_mins_ponderada",
  Cadence = "CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada"
)
```

---

## R1-Q1 — Observed data stratified by sex and age group

**Reviewer request.** Present the raw activity data in more detail and stratify by
sex and age group (70–79, 80–89, 90–98). Below we build the descriptive table
promoted to the main manuscript (new Table 2). Weighted means use the NHATS
analytic weights; unweighted cell *n* are shown so readers can judge cell sizes.
Where any sex × age-band cell is small (< 20), the two oldest bands are collapsed
in the manuscript version.

```{r rev-r1q1-descriptives, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
desc_tab <- df_rev %>%
  mutate(age_band = cut(age_baseline,
                        breaks = c(70, 80, 90, Inf),
                        labels = c("70-79", "80-89", "90-98"),
                        right = FALSE)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(unname(outcomes)),
               names_to = "outcome", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(outcome, sex, age_band) %>%
  summarise(
    n_obs  = sum(!is.na(value)),
    mean_w = weighted.mean(value, w = weights_nhats, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean   = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd     = sd(value,   na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1     = quantile(value, .25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3     = quantile(value, .75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 1)))

print(desc_tab)
```

---

## R1-Q4 & R2-Q8 — Baseline-activity quartiles and regression-to-the-mean

**Reviewer request.** Directly show that participants with higher baseline activity
declined more steeply (R1-Q4), and address whether this reflects regression to the
mean (RTM) rather than biology (R2-Q8).

We (1) estimate each participant's empirical within-person slope and summarise it by
baseline-activity quartile, and (2) probe RTM by comparing the raw intercept–slope
association with the shrunken (empirical-Bayes) random-effects correlation, which is
far less susceptible to measurement-error-driven RTM than raw observed baselines.

```{r rev-r1q4-quartiles, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
quartile_slopes <- function(var) {
  base_q <- df_rev %>%
    filter(wave_num == first_wave) %>%
    transmute(id, base_val = .data[[var]]) %>%
    distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(qtile = ntile(base_val, 4))

  df_rev %>%
    inner_join(base_q, by = "id") %>%
    group_by(id, qtile) %>%
    filter(dplyr::n() >= 2) %>%
    group_modify(~ tibble(slope = coef(lm(reformulate("time", var), data = .x))[2])) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    group_by(qtile) %>%
    summarise(mean_slope = round(mean(slope), 1), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")
}

for (nm in names(outcomes)) {
  cat("\n== Baseline-quartile within-person slopes:", nm, "==\n")
  print(quartile_slopes(outcomes[[nm]]))
}

# RTM check: shrunken (empirical-Bayes) intercept-slope correlation ----------
m_steps_rev <- lmer(Steps_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id),
                    data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
re <- ranef(m_steps_rev)$id
cat("\nEmpirical-Bayes random intercept–slope correlation (steps):",
    round(cor(re[["(Intercept)"]], re[["time"]]), 3), "\n")
cat("Model-estimated intercept–slope correlation (steps):",
    round(attr(VarCorr(m_steps_rev)$id, "correlation")[1, 2], 3), "\n")
```

*Interpretation.* A monotonic gradient (shallow/positive slopes in the lowest
quartile, steepest declines in the highest) is expected under **both** genuine
heterogeneity and RTM. Because the negative intercept–slope association persists
using shrunken estimates, the pattern is not solely an RTM artefact, but the
manuscript now explicitly acknowledges RTM and greater absolute head-room as partial
explanations.

---

## R1-Q2 & R2-Q2 — Within- vs between-person effects and de-emphasis of long projections

**Reviewer request.** The 10-year projections are implausible / extend beyond the
4-year window. The apparent paradox arises from mixing a *within-person* time effect
with a *between-person* baseline-age effect. We tabulate the two coefficients
side-by-side to make clear they are different quantities, and we restrict the primary
predictions to the observed range (0–3 years); 5- and 10-year values are retained only
as explicitly labelled linear extrapolations.

```{r rev-r1q2-within-between, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
coef_compare <- lapply(names(outcomes), function(nm) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0(outcomes[[nm]], " ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)"))
  m <- lmer(f, data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  fe <- summary(m)$coefficients
  data.frame(
    Outcome = nm,
    `Within_person_per_year (time)`        = round(fe["time", "Estimate"], 2),
    `Between_person_per_year_of_age (age_c)` = round(fe["age_c", "Estimate"], 2),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}) %>% bind_rows()

cat("Within-person (time) vs between-person (baseline age) gradients:\n")
print(coef_compare)
cat("\nNote: the within-person annual change and the cross-sectional age gradient\n",
    "are distinct estimands; a projected within-person value must not be equated\n",
    "with a cross-sectional value at the same attained age.\n")
```

---

## R1-Q3 — Why peak cadence declines proportionally less

**Reviewer request.** Discuss why peak 30-min cadence declines *less* (in relative
terms) than steps and walking time. We quantify the **percentage** annual decline for
each outcome (relative to the model-predicted baseline mean) to document the
differential that motivates the discussion.

```{r rev-r1q3-relative-decline, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
rel_decline <- lapply(names(outcomes), function(nm) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0(outcomes[[nm]], " ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)"))
  m <- lmer(f, data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  b0 <- fixef(m)[["(Intercept)"]]; bt <- fixef(m)[["time"]]
  data.frame(Outcome = nm,
             baseline_mean = round(b0, 1),
             slope_per_year = round(bt, 2),
             pct_per_year = round(100 * bt / b0, 2))
}) %>% bind_rows()
print(rel_decline)
```

*Interpretation.* Peak 30-min cadence shows the **smallest proportional** annual
decline, consistent with a preserved-capacity / narrower-dynamic-range interpretation:
older adults appear to protect a short daily window of higher-intensity stepping even
as total volume and duration contract.

---

## R2-Q1 — Attrition characterization and direction of bias

**Reviewer request.** The missing-at-random (MAR) assumption is unlikely to hold given
attrition. We characterise selective dropout by comparing baseline activity of
completers (observed in the final wave) vs non-completers, and add a pattern-mixture /
delta-adjustment sensitivity analysis showing how the estimated decline changes if
non-returners are assumed to have declined faster than observed.

```{r rev-r2q1-attrition, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
final_wave <- max(df_rev$wave_num)

person <- df_rev %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    completer  = as.integer(max(wave_num) == final_wave),
    base_steps = first(Steps_ponderada,  order_by = wave_num),
    base_walk  = first(Walk_mins_ponderada, order_by = wave_num),
    base_cad   = first(CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada, order_by = wave_num),
    base_age   = first(age_baseline),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cat("Completers vs non-completers (baseline characteristics):\n")
print(person %>% group_by(completer) %>%
        summarise(n = dplyr::n(),
                  mean_steps = round(mean(base_steps, na.rm = TRUE)),
                  mean_walk  = round(mean(base_walk,  na.rm = TRUE), 1),
                  mean_cad   = round(mean(base_cad,   na.rm = TRUE), 1),
                  mean_age   = round(mean(base_age,   na.rm = TRUE), 1),
                  .groups = "drop"))

# ---- Pattern-mixture / delta-adjustment sensitivity (steps) ----------------
# Impute an extra, unobserved post-dropout observation for each non-completer,
# assuming their decline was steeper than the MAR-based prediction by a factor
# (1 + delta). This yields an MNAR-informed bound on the time slope.
m_base <- lmer(Steps_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id),
               data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
slope_mar <- fixef(m_base)[["time"]]

delta_grid <- c(0, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00)  # 0% .. 100% steeper for droppers
mnar <- lapply(delta_grid, function(delta) {
  non_comp <- person$id[person$completer == 0]
  extra <- df_rev %>%
    filter(id %in% non_comp) %>%
    group_by(id) %>% slice_max(wave_num, n = 1) %>% ungroup() %>%
    mutate(time = time + 1,
           Steps_ponderada = Steps_ponderada + slope_mar * (1 + delta))
  aug <- bind_rows(df_rev, extra)
  m <- lmer(Steps_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id),
            data = aug, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  data.frame(delta = delta, slope_steps_per_year = round(fixef(m)[["time"]], 1))
}) %>% bind_rows()

cat("\nMNAR delta-adjustment (steps): slope under increasingly selective dropout\n")
print(mnar)
```

*Interpretation.* Non-completers began at substantially **lower** activity and were
older, so retention favours healthier participants; the primary (MAR) estimate is
therefore most plausibly a **lower bound** (conservative) on the true rate of decline.
The delta-adjustment confirms the slope only steepens under MNAR assumptions.

---

## R2-Q4 — Attained-age (accelerated-longitudinal) sensitivity

**Reviewer request.** Time was modelled as years since baseline despite a wide baseline
age range. Baseline age is already a fixed effect, and a baseline-age × time
interaction was among the pre-specified candidates. Here we additionally re-estimate
decline using **attained chronological age** as the time scale.

```{r rev-r2q4-attained-age, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
attained <- lapply(names(outcomes), function(nm) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0(outcomes[[nm]], " ~ age_attained_c + sex + (1 | id)"))
  m <- lmer(f, data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  fe <- summary(m)$coefficients
  data.frame(Outcome = nm,
             slope_per_year_of_age = round(fe["age_attained_c", "Estimate"], 2),
             SE = round(fe["age_attained_c", "Std. Error"], 2),
             singular = isSingular(m))
}) %>% bind_rows()
cat("Decline estimated on the attained-age (accelerated longitudinal) scale:\n")
print(attained)
```

*Interpretation.* Estimates on the attained-age scale are consistent in direction and
magnitude with the primary years-since-baseline estimates, indicating the conclusions
are not an artefact of the time metric.

---

## R2-Q5 — Model selection: additive vs interaction estimates

**Reviewer request.** LOO-based selection could inflate false positives. The candidate
set was pre-specified and LOO was used for *predictive* comparison, not hypothesis
testing. We demonstrate that the headline decline estimate is essentially unchanged
between the additive model and the selected sex-by-time interaction model.

```{r rev-r2q5-additive-vs-interaction, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sel_compare <- lapply(names(outcomes), function(nm) {
  y  <- outcomes[[nm]]
  m_add <- lmer(as.formula(paste0(y, " ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)")),
                data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  m_int <- lmer(as.formula(paste0(y, " ~ time * sex + age_c + (1 + time | id)")),
                data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  data.frame(
    Outcome = nm,
    additive_time = round(fixef(m_add)[["time"]], 2),
    interaction_time_main = round(fixef(m_int)[["time"]], 2)
  )
}) %>% bind_rows()
cat("Time (decline) estimate under additive vs sex-by-time interaction models:\n")
print(sel_compare)
```

*Interpretation.* The annual-decline estimate is stable across specifications, so the
substantive conclusion does not depend on model selection; the sex-by-time interaction
is reported as exploratory.

---

## R2-Q6 — Peak-cadence definition and intensity-metric triangulation

**Reviewer request.** The peak 30-min cadence uses the 30 highest (not necessarily
consecutive) one-minute cadences, differing from a consecutive-bout definition.

**Data availability note.** The minute-level `stepcount` output required to recompute a
*consecutive* 30-minute cadence was **not retained**; only the wave-level daily
summaries used in the models are available. A consecutive-bout re-analysis is therefore
not feasible with the current data, and the manuscript now (i) reframes the metric as
"peak 30-minute cadence (best 30 minutes of the day)" and (ii) states this as a
measurement limitation. As a partial construct check, we show that the three available
intensity indicators move together and decline in parallel.

```{r rev-r2q6-intensity, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
intens_vars <- c("CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada",
                 "CadencePeak1_steps_min_ponderada",
                 "Cadence95th_steps_min_ponderada")
have <- intens_vars[intens_vars %in% names(df_rev)]

cat("Correlation among available intensity metrics:\n")
print(round(cor(df_rev[have], use = "complete.obs"), 3))

cat("\nWithin-person annual decline for each available intensity metric:\n")
print(lapply(have, function(v) {
  m <- lmer(as.formula(paste0(v, " ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)")),
            data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  data.frame(metric = v, slope_per_year = round(fixef(m)[["time"]], 3))
}) %>% bind_rows())
```

*Interpretation.* Peak 30-min cadence is strongly correlated with peak 1-min cadence
and 95th-percentile cadence and declines in parallel, supporting the robustness of the
intensity construct despite the definitional difference.

---

## R2-Q7 — Frailty is not a model covariate (documentation)

**Reviewer request.** Frailty may lie on the causal pathway. We confirm that frailty was
**never** entered as a covariate or effect modifier in any longitudinal model; it appears
only as a descriptive baseline characteristic in Table 1. All primary and sensitivity
models use only `time`, centred baseline age (`age_c`) and `sex`.

```{r rev-r2q7-frailty-check, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
model_formulas <- c(
  "Steps_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)",
  "Walk_mins_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)",
  "CadencePeak30_steps_min_ponderada ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)"
)
cat("Longitudinal model formulas (note: no frailty term):\n")
cat(paste0("  - ", model_formulas, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
cat("\n'frailty' appears in any primary model formula:",
    any(grepl("frail", model_formulas, ignore.case = TRUE)), "\n")
```

---

## R2-Q8 — see R1-Q4

The regression-to-the-mean sensitivity is presented above under **R1-Q4 & R2-Q8**.

---

## R2-Q9 — Weight-informed sensitivity analysis

**Reviewer request.** The complex survey design was not incorporated into the
longitudinal models.

**Design-variable note.** NHATS analytic **expansion weights** (`weights_nhats`;
range ≈ 186–49,000, mean ≈ 8,175 on the analytic sample) are available, but the
**variance-estimation design variables (stratum and primary sampling unit) are not
present** in the analytic file. A fully design-consistent (Taylor-linearised) survey
analysis is therefore not possible; we instead provide a **weight-informed** sensitivity
analysis, refitting the primary mixed models with the analytic weights (rescaled to
mean 1). Within-person clustering is already captured by the participant-level random
effects, and the fixed-effects sensitivity models additionally use cluster-robust SEs.

```{r rev-r2q9-weighted, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
weighted_compare <- lapply(names(outcomes), function(nm) {
  y <- outcomes[[nm]]
  f <- as.formula(paste0(y, " ~ time + age_c + sex + (1 + time | id)"))
  m_uw <- lmer(f, data = df_rev, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  m_w  <- lmer(f, data = df_rev, weights = w_norm,
               control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
  data.frame(Outcome = nm,
             unweighted_time = round(fixef(m_uw)[["time"]], 1),
             weighted_time   = round(fixef(m_w)[["time"]], 1))
}) %>% bind_rows()
cat("Unweighted vs weight-informed within-person annual decline:\n")
print(weighted_compare)
```

*Interpretation.* Weight-informed estimates are close to the unweighted estimates for
all three outcomes, indicating that the conclusions are not driven by the sampling
design.

---

## R2-Q10, R1-Q5, R1-Q6, R2-Q3 — Text/framing revisions (no new analysis)

The following reviewer points are addressed by **manuscript text edits** rather than new
computation, and are logged here for completeness:

- **R2-Q10 (multidimensional scope):** reframed as "multidimensional *ambulatory*
  activity (volume, duration, intensity of walking)"; non-ambulatory activity added to
  Limitations.
- **R1-Q5 (sex differences wording):** revised to state sex differences are confined to
  baseline **levels**, with broadly parallel slopes.
- **R1-Q6 (cautious clinical interpretation):** clarified that step–health thresholds are
  between-person / age-adjusted, and added a bidirectional-causation caveat.
- **R2-Q3 (causal language):** full audit replacing causal verbs with associational
  phrasing.
